map.area: Write path: frames into the ring buffer (SkellyCam)
map.summary: Each camera runs in its own OS process (WorkerMode.PROCESS in both SkellyCam's and FreeMoCap's __main__). Each process owns one cv2.VideoCapture (DSHOW on Windows, MJPG capture, CAP_PROP_BUFFERSIZE=1) and runs a lockstep grab -> retrieve -> put_frame -> (optional) encode-to-disk loop. The parent process (CameraGroup.start) creates one SharedMemoryRingBuffer per camera: a single pagefile-backed numpy recarray of 1 GiB // record_size slots (388 slots at 720p, 172 at 1080p), where each record is 632 B of aligned metadata followed by the HxWx3 uint8 image. The read/write indices are separate int64 SharedMemoryNumber segments. The camera process attaches through a DTO sent over a multiprocessing.Queue. cv2 decodes into a process-private recarray, verified in place for matching shapes. put_data then makes two full-frame copies: copy.copy(), which is a wasted heap copy, and the slot assignment into shm. It then stores last_written_index, with overwrite always allowed. There is no lock, seqlock or fence: the writer only orders "slot then index" in program order, and a reader that lags near the overwrite edge can get torn frames that the frame-number checks do not catch (this was reproduced). Multi-camera sync is not enforced at write time. Each camera may only grab when its frame_count is <= every other camera's, and readers take min(last_written_index) and check that frame numbers match. Disk recording happens synchronously inside the camera loop, from the private recarray and not from shm, before frame_count is published, so the slowest encoder gates every camera.

claims.statement: Camera workers are separate OS processes in production: SkellyCam's __main__ builds WorkerRegistry(worker_mode=WorkerMode.PROCESS), and FreeMoCap's __main__ does the same. create_worker instantiates ManagedProcess (multiprocessing.Process) for PROCESS mode and ManagedThread only for THREAD mode, which is used in FreeMoCap tests.

There is one worker per camera, with target opencv_camera_worker_method and name Camera{index}-{id}-Worker. CameraManager.start launches the workers one after another, sleeping 0.25 s between spawns on Windows.

Capture backend: OpenCV only. On Windows it is cv2.CAP_DSHOW, on Linux CAP_V4L2, on macOS AVFoundation. Each process opens cv2.VideoCapture(index, backend), sets FOURCC (default 'MJPG'), width/height and FPS, and requests CAP_PROP_BUFFERSIZE=1. The default resolution is 1280x720x3.

Shared memory is created by the parent process, not by the cameras. CameraGroup.start waits for each camera's extracted config, then calls CameraGroupSharedMemory.create(..., read_only=True) and publishes the DTO on the SHM_UPDATES topic. Each topic subscription is a multiprocessing.Queue, so the DTO is pickled.

The camera process attaches as the writer. It polls shm_subscription every 10 ms, takes its own DTO from SetShmMessage, and calls CameraSharedMemoryRingBuffer.recreate(dto, read_only=False). It then flushes frames with cap.read() until orchestrator.all_ready, and only then builds its private frame_rec_array.

Slot count: SharedMemoryRingBuffer.create defaults memory_allocation to ONE_GIGABYTE and sets ring_buffer_length = memory_allocation // record itemsize. CameraSharedMemoryRingBuffer.from_config does not override this. Measured: 388 slots at 1280x720 (6.47 s of history at 60 fps) and 172 slots at 1920x1080 (2.87 s), i.e. about 1 GiB of shm per camera (5 GiB for 5 cameras).

Record layout: the frame dtype is an aligned struct of ('frame_metadata', FRAME_METADATA_DTYPE) followed by ('image', uint8, (H, W, C)). The metadata holds camera_info (camera_id 'U128', index, rotation, channels), frame_number int64, timebase_mapping, and 9 int64 lifecycle timestamps. Measured: metadata is 632 B, the image starts at offset 632, and the record is 2,765,432 B at 720p and 6,221,432 B at 1080p. The 'U128' camera_id alone is 512 B.

Each SharedMemoryElement allocates 3 shm segments: data, a 1-byte valid flag, and a 1-byte first_data_written flag. A ring buffer is one element plus two SharedMemoryNumbers (also elements), so each camera uses 9 named segments. The buffer is a numpy recarray viewing shm.buf directly; exp1 confirms np.shares_memory is True. On Windows, CPython creates each segment with CreateFileMapping(INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE, PAGE_READWRITE, size), i.e. pagefile-backed.

claims.statement: Write call chain per frame, in the camera process: run_opencv_camera_loop calls camera_loop_update_checks (recording-info, config and pause queues), then checks should_close / is_paused, then orchestrator.should_grab_by_id (wait_10us and retry if False), then sets grabbing_frame=True, then opencv_get_frame in a retry loop of up to 30 attempts, then orchestrator.should_record_frame_number, then sets grabbing_frame=False. It then stamps pre_copy_to_camera_shm_ns, calls camera_shm.put_frame(overwrite=True), and stamps post_copy_to_camera_shm_ns. After that come handle_video_recording, check_framerate_reset, initialize_frame_recarray, and finally self_status.frame_count.value = frame_number.

opencv_get_frame: timestamps around cap.grab(), then cap.retrieve(image=frame_rec_array.image[0]), where the returned array is discarded with '_'. It then increments frame_metadata.frame_number and draws a text overlay in place with two cv2.putText calls.

frame_rec_array is a process-private np.recarray created by create_initial_frame_rec_array, not a view into shm. cv2 therefore decodes into private memory, and the image has to be copied into shm afterwards.

When the preallocated view matches the stream size, cap.retrieve(image=view) writes into it in place: the returned array shares memory with the view and the pointer is unchanged. The view is C-contiguous and writeable. Verified with the FFMPEG file backend in cv2 4.12.0, not with DSHOW.

If the preallocated view has the wrong shape, OpenCV allocates a new array and leaves the provided buffer untouched (exp2: 640x480 buffer with a 1280x720 or 1920x1080 stream gives ok=True and the buffer stays all zero). opencv_get_frame discards that return value. So if a resolution change is applied in place (check_for_new_config -> apply_camera_configuration sets CAP_PROP_FRAME_WIDTH/HEIGHT) without rebuilding frame_rec_array and the shm, stale pixels would be published and recorded silently.

put_frame calls put_data(overwrite_allowed=overwrite), and the camera loop always passes overwrite=True. The overwrite guard (_check_for_overwrite against last_read_index) is therefore never active on the live write path, and the writer never waits for readers.

put_data does `self.ring_shm.buffer[index % L] = copy(data)` and then sets `last_written_index.value = index`. copy.copy() of an ndarray is a full data copy: exp1 shows shares_memory False and a tracemalloc peak of 1.0 x the record size per put. The assignment is a second full copy into shm. Every frame is therefore copied twice inside put_data, and the copy.copy one is unnecessary.

Measured put_frame cost (Python 3.12.13, numpy 2.2.6, this PC). Steady state: median 0.652 ms at 720p and 1.400 ms at 1080p. First lap (fresh shm pages): 1.260 ms and 2.823 ms. Of the steady-state time, copy.copy takes 0.392 / 0.901 ms and the slot assignment 0.243 / 0.457 ms. A single np.copyto(buf[s:s+1], frame) took 0.100 / 0.217 ms, measured right after writing the same slot, so possibly cache-warm.

Index handling: last_written_index and last_read_index are monotonically increasing int64 counters, each in its own SharedMemoryNumber segment and starting at -1. The physical slot is index % ring_buffer_length, so wraparound is purely modular and the counters never reset. SharedMemoryNumber.value set builds a new 1-element recarray and np.copyto's it. get goes through retrieve_data, which re-reads the valid and first_data_written flags and copies via np.rec.array. Measured cost is about 4.4 us per set and 5.8 us per get.

last_read_index is never advanced in production. The only consumer is get_next_data / retrieve_next_frame, and nothing outside tests and the module's __main__ demo calls either. The parent creates the buffer read_only=True, and get_next_data raises on read-only instances. So last_read_index stays -1, and new_data_available / new_data_indicies are meaningless for the live system.

Synchronisation: the ring write path has no lock, seqlock, generation counter or memory fence. The only ordering is Python program order: the slot memcpy happens before the index store. Readers in get_data_by_index check staleness (current_write_head - index >= L) before the copy, and never re-check afterwards.

Torn reads are possible and are not always detected. In a cross-process test (unthrottled writer at about 1,350-1,500 fps, 720p), reading the oldest valid index of a 2-slot ring gave 5,520 frame-number mismatches and 15 silent tears (correct frame_number, mixed pixels). A latest read on a 2-slot ring gave 1 silent tear. With the production 388-slot ring and latest reads, 0 of 7,706 reads were bad. The reader-side frame-number check in get_images_by_frame_number only logs a warning, and neither check can catch a tear where the metadata is old and the pixels are partly new.

Multi-camera sync is enforced before the grab, not at write time. should_grab_by_id returns True only if all cameras are ready and this camera's frame_count is <= every other camera's frame_count. frame_count is a multiprocessing.Value('q') per camera, read through a deepcopied dict. Each camera publishes frame_count only at the very end of its loop iteration, so no camera can start frame N+1 until every camera has finished frame N, including its put and video write.

The multi-frame is assembled on the read side. latest_multiframe_number = min(last_written_index across cameras), and get_latest_multiframe copies that index from every camera and raises ValueError if the frame_numbers differ. This relies on the invariant slot index == frame_number. Both start at -1 and advance by 1 per successful frame (put at index 0 carries frame_number 0).

The slot-index == frame_number invariant can break. If all 30 retries fail (or should_continue goes False), the retry loop exits with frame_success False, and the loop still calls put_frame and handle_video_recording with the unchanged frame_number. last_written_index advances while frame_number does not. If recording, VideoRecorder._validate_frame_number then raises because the frame numbers are not consecutive, the exception handler calls ipc.kill_everything(), and the whole app shuts down.

Disk recording does not read the ring buffer. handle_video_recording passes the camera's private frame_rec_array to VideoRecorder.record_frame, which calls video_writer.write(image) synchronously inside the capture loop. The writer is cv2.VideoWriter (default fourcc X264) or PyavVideoWriter. This happens after put_frame and before frame_count is published.

Recording start and stop are frame-number based. While all cameras are paused, the parent sets first_recording_frame_number = max(frame_count) + 3 (or last_recording_frame_number for stop). Each camera decides should_record_frame from its own frame_number before clearing grabbing_frame. All cameras therefore record the same frame range, but capture stops while paused for every start and stop.

The gating spin is coarser than its name suggests. wait_10us is time.sleep(1e-5), but on this Windows machine it measured a median of 526 us (p95 563 us). wait_1ms measured a median of 1,090 us. A gated camera therefore re-checks roughly every 0.5 ms.

Per-iteration overhead beyond the frame work: ipc.should_continue reads two Synchronized flags and the heartbeat Value. camera_loop_update_checks polls two multiprocessing.Queue.empty() calls. should_grab_by_id reads N+1 status Values per camera per attempt. The skellycam package runs beartype_this_package() at import, so every annotated function on the hot path (put_frame, opencv_get_frame, and others) is wrapped with runtime type checks. The beartype failure in exp1's first attempt shows the checks are active.

The existing tests for this layer (test_shared_memory.py) are single-process. They use a 24-byte dtype and a 5-slot ring, and cover create, DTO round-trip, put/get, overwrite protection and index bounds. Nothing tests image-sized records, concurrent writer/reader processes, torn reads, the copy.copy cost, or multi-camera alignment at write time. They pass (39 passed together with test_camera_orchestrator.py), but only with --noconftest, because conftest imports polars, which is missing from the skellycam venv.

The diagnostic skellycam/system/diagnostics/check_shm_speed.py is stale and does not run. It imports SharedMemoryRingBufferDTO from the empty package __init__ (ImportError), and it uses APIs that no longer exist: example_payload=, get_next_payload, get_latest_payload, ring_buffer_shape, last_read_index.get(). It cannot be used as a throughput baseline.

Spawned child processes that import skellycam.core.types.type_overloads fail unless multiprocessing.queues was already imported. The module references multiprocessing.queues.Queue but only imports multiprocessing.sharedctypes. exp3's first run failed in the child with AttributeError until the script pre-imported multiprocessing.queues. In production, import order presumably hides this.

frame_copies.where: Inside the capture backend (DSHOW MJPEG decompressor / videoInput sample buffer) before the pixels reach the Python-provided Mat
frame_copies.necessary: An MJPEG-to-BGR decode is unavoidable with MJPG capture. Whether DSHOW also does an internal sample-buffer to Mat memcpy was not verified (no camera available, and the OpenCV cap_dshow source was not read). Listed as an open question.

frame_copies.where: cap.retrieve(image=frame_rec_array.image[0]) writes decoded BGR into the camera process's private recarray
frame_copies.necessary: Some decode output write is necessary. Putting it in private memory, rather than in the shm slot itself, is what makes copy #2 below necessary. Decoding directly into a view of the next shm slot (retrieve accepts a preallocated contiguous view, exp2) would remove the later copies. That needs a slot-reservation or seqlock protocol, because readers could see a half-decoded slot.

frame_copies.where: draw_doubled_text: two cv2.putText calls stamp the camera id and frame number onto the image in place
frame_copies.kind: other (in-place pixel modification, not a copy)
frame_copies.necessary: Not a copy, but it alters the recorded and analysed pixels in the top-left region (the overlay is burned into the saved videos). It is optional and debug-like.

frame_copies.where: SharedMemoryRingBuffer.put_data: copy(data), i.e. copy.copy of the full recarray (metadata + image) into a new heap array
frame_copies.kind: numpy copy (full record, plus heap allocation of 2.7 / 6.2 MB per frame)
frame_copies.necessary: Unnecessary. The source is already process-private and is not mutated during the assignment. It costs a median 0.39 ms (720p) or 0.90 ms (1080p) and about 60% of put_frame time (exp1b). It can be removed by assigning or np.copyto'ing data directly into the slot.

frame_copies.where: SharedMemoryRingBuffer.put_data: ring_shm.buffer[index % L] = <temp>, which copies into the shm slot
frame_copies.necessary: Necessary in the current design, where decode happens into private memory. It could be avoided by decoding straight into the slot (see the retrieve entry). It costs 0.24 ms (720p) or 0.46 ms (1080p) steady state, and more on the first lap because of page faults on fresh shm pages.

frame_copies.where: VideoRecorder.record_frame: cv2.rotate(frame.image[0], rotation) when a rotation is configured
frame_copies.necessary: Only happens when rotation != -1. It could be avoided by writing unrotated video plus a rotation flag in the metadata or container.

frame_copies.where: VideoRecorder.record_frame: video_writer.write(image), with cv2.VideoWriter (X264 default) or PyavVideoWriter, where av.VideoFrame.from_ndarray copies the input
frame_copies.kind: encode (plus a PyAV from_ndarray copy, verified)
frame_copies.necessary: Encoding is required for disk writes. The from_ndarray copy is a PyAV API property (exp: modifying the input after from_ndarray does not change the frame). The encode runs synchronously in the capture loop.

frame_copies.where: VideoRecorder.record_frame: video_frame_metadata.append(copy(frame.frame_metadata))
frame_copies.kind: numpy copy (metadata only, 632 B, not the image)
frame_copies.necessary: Small. It accumulates per-frame metadata in RAM for the timestamp CSVs and is not an image copy.

frame_copies.where: Setup only: cap.read() in the all_ready flush loop allocates a new frame per call, and create_initial_frame_rec_array builds np.zeros(...) + camera_index temporaries
frame_copies.kind: numpy allocation/copy (one-time, not per steady-state frame)
frame_copies.necessary: One-time startup cost. Not on the hot path.

flow_steps.action: Spawn one camera worker process per camera (0.25 s stagger on Windows)
Open cv2.VideoCapture(index, DSHOW), set MJPG/resolution/FPS/BUFFERSIZE=1, publish DeviceExtractedConfigMessage
await_extracted_configs, then CameraGroupSharedMemory.create(read_only=True) allocates a 1 GiB ring + 2 index numbers per camera, then publish SetShmMessage(DTO) through multiprocessing.Queue
CameraSharedMemoryRingBuffer.recreate(dto, read_only=False), set connected=True, flush with cap.read() until all cameras are ready, build the private frame_rec_array
camera_loop_update_checks (recording info / config / pause queues), should_close and is_paused checks
Lockstep gate: should_grab_by_id is true only if own frame_count <= every other camera's frame_count (else sleep(1e-5), about 0.5 ms on Windows)
cap.grab() (timestamped), cap.retrieve(image=private view) to decode MJPEG to BGR in place, frame_number += 1, putText overlay
should_record_frame_number(frame_number), then grabbing_frame=False
put_frame(overwrite=True): dtype check, copy.copy(frame) (heap copy), buffer[idx % L] = tmp (shm copy), last_written_index.value = idx
If recording: VideoRecorder.record_frame(private frame_rec_array), with optional cv2.rotate copy, then synchronous VideoWriter.write encode to disk
check_framerate_reset (may release and reopen the capture), reset timestamps, publish frame_count = frame_number, which releases the other cameras' gate
latest_multiframe_number = min(last_written_index), get_data_by_index per camera (copies out), frame_number equality check

risks_for_priorities.risk: Disk encode is synchronous in each camera's capture loop and finishes before frame_count is published. The lockstep gate means the slowest encoder throttles every camera. With CAP_PROP_BUFFERSIZE=1, frames the sensor delivers while the loop is busy are dropped by the driver or backend. frame_number counts retrieved frames, not sensor frames, so _validate_frame_number cannot detect these drops, and the video silently contains fewer real-time frames than were exposed.

After 30 consecutive grab/retrieve failures the loop still puts and records a frame with an unchanged frame_number. During a recording this raises a non-consecutive-frame ValueError, which calls kill_everything and kills the entire app mid-recording.

check_framerate_reset releases and recreates the VideoCapture inside the loop after more than 30 consecutive frames slower than 2/30 s. Its threshold is hard-coded to 30 fps (66.7 ms), whatever the real target rate. While the device reopens, no frames are captured for this camera and, through the gate, none for any camera.
Recording start and stop pause all cameras, so frames are not captured during the transition (by design, but it is a capture gap).

Strict lockstep: no camera can begin frame N+1 until all cameras finish grab, decode, put, encode and the frame_count store for frame N. Group throughput is therefore bounded by the slowest camera's whole serial loop body, plus about 0.5 ms of polling granularity (wait_10us measured at 526 us median).

put_frame costs 1.4 ms per 1080p frame in steady state and 2.8 ms on the first lap through fresh shm pages. That is 8-17% of the 16.7 ms frame budget at 60 fps, spent serially in every camera's loop. About 60% of it is the redundant copy.copy.

1 GiB of pagefile-backed shm per camera (5 GiB for 5 cameras), whatever the resolution. Combined with first-touch page faults, this raises startup and commit pressure. At 1080p the history is only 2.87 s, which bounds how far any reader may lag before its data is overwritten.
beartype_this_package() instruments every hot-path call in the skellycam package (cost not measured here). LOG_LEVEL is TRACE at import.

At least two full-frame copies per frame on the way in (decode into private memory, then copy.copy, then the slot copy), plus a rotate copy when rotation is set and PyAV's from_ndarray copy on Linux. At 5 x 1080p x 60 fps, each extra full-frame copy is about 1.87 GB/s of memory writes.

Decoding straight into the shm slot, which would remove copies, is unsafe with the current protocol. There is no seqlock or slot-ownership flag, and readers already see silent torn frames near the overwrite edge (exp3). Zero-copy needs a commit protocol, such as per-slot sequence numbers written before and after the slot and re-checked by readers.

A reader that falls behind is only detected by a stale-index check before the copy and a frame_number check after it (there is no seqlock). It takes the "latest complete multiframe" (min of the per-camera write heads), copies each camera's slot out of SHM (1 full-frame copy per camera), then resizes, JPEG-encodes and assembles a bytearray (another full-payload copy). The ring buffer has three read APIs. get_next_data is the only one that advances last_read_index (consuming read). get_latest_data and get_data_by_index are non-consuming. All three copy the slot into a private recarray with np.copyto and never return a view of SHM. get_next_data also refuses to run on a read_only instance.

No production code calls get_next_data or retrieve_next_frame. Across skellycam/, the only callers are the module's __main__ demo, tests and a broken diagnostic. The real readers are get_latest_multiframe and get_images_by_frame_number (both built on get_data_by_index), plus FreeMoCap's direct get_data_by_index calls. last_read_index therefore stays at -1 for the whole session.
The producer always writes with overwrite=True, so _check_for_overwrite never blocks or raises. Readers cannot apply back-pressure to the camera, and a lagging reader is overwritten silently.

Ring depth is memory_allocation (default 1 GiB) // frame itemsize, per camera. Measured: 388 slots at 1280x720 BGR (itemsize 2,765,432 B, about 6.47 s at 60 fps) and 172 slots at 1920x1080 (itemsize 6,221,432 B, about 2.87 s at 60 fps). Each camera's segment is about 1.07 GB, so 5 cameras need about 5.4 GB of shared memory. Source: scratchpad read_path_probe_output.txt lines 23 and 36, from `C:/Users/Dom/GitHub/freemocap/skellycam/.venv/Scripts/python.exe read_path_probe.py`.

Ring index equals frame_number. The write index starts at last_written_index(-1)+1 = 0. frame_number starts at -1 and is incremented once per successful retrieve, before the single put per loop iteration. So readers address frames by ring index: get_data_by_index(index=frame_number).

Lag detection in get_data_by_index happens only BEFORE the copy: it raises IndexError if write_head - index >= ring_length. Nothing re-checks the write head after the np.copyto, and there is no sequence lock. A writer that laps the slot during the copy can produce a torn image. The docstring hands verification to the caller, who is told to compare frame_number. Because metadata sits ahead of the image in the record, a matching frame_number does not prove the image bytes are consistent (this is a structural inference; no torn read was reproduced).

The disk writer (VideoRecorder) is not a ring-buffer reader. In the camera loop, put_frame(frame_rec_array) is followed directly by handle_video_recording(frame_rec_array=...). The recorder encodes the camera process's own local recarray, not the SHM slot. Probe check: np.shares_memory(frame.image[0], SHM ring) is False, and np.shares_memory(frame.image[0], local recarray) is True (read_path_probe_output.txt line 28).

The recorder runs in the camera worker. In standalone SkellyCam that is a separate OS process per camera (WorkerMode.PROCESS in __main__). There is no recorder thread, queue or process: encoding is synchronous in the grab loop, one VideoRecorder per camera.

Writer selection: VideoRecorder.create resolves a fourcc via resolve_writer_fourcc. The order is: the requested fourcc (default 'X264'), then X264/H264/avc1/pyav-libx264, then mp4v/XVID/MJPG. The framerate is the measured median capture framerate when available.

On this machine (opencv 4.12.0, SkellyCam venv), cv2.VideoWriter with 'X264', 'H264' or 'avc1' opens on the MSMF (Windows Media Foundation) backend, not FFmpeg. record_frame hands the encoder a view: frame.image[0], which is C-contiguous and not a copy (probe line 28). It allocates a new rotated image with cv2.rotate only when camera_info.rotation != -1. Writer-side gap detection: _validate_frame_number raises ValueError if a frame is not previous+1. The exception reaches the camera loop's except block, which calls ipc.kill_everything(). Upstream frame loss is silent by design. The capture is opened with CAP_PROP_BUFFERSIZE=1 on DSHOW (the Windows backend), so grab() returns the most recent driver frame. If the loop, including the synchronous encode, runs slower than the sensor, older frames are discarded in the driver with no counter. The only trace is timing in the per-frame timestamps.

The recorder throttles all cameras, not only its own. A camera may grab only when its frame_count <= every other camera's (lockstep), and frame_count is updated only after handle_video_recording returns. One camera's slow write() therefore delays the next grab of every camera.

Recording start is applied by frame number. start_recording does the following in order: pause all cameras and wait; set last_recording_frame_number=-1 and first_recording_frame_number=max(frame_count)+3; publish RecordingInfoMessage; await 10 ms; unpause. should_record_frame_number returns True for frame_number >= first.

Each camera builds its VideoRecorder in its own process when it dequeues RecordingInfoMessage from its own multiprocessing.Queue subscription. This happens in camera_loop_update_checks, which runs before the pause check, so it also runs while paused. Creation includes codec probing that writes a temp file. The camera then busy-waits until all cameras report recording_in_progress. If the message has not been consumed by the time the camera reaches first_recording_frame_number, handle_video_recording raises RuntimeError('Record requested before video_recorder was created'). That is a crash, not a silent drop.

Recording stop is also frame-number based. stop_recording pauses; sets first=-1 and last=max(frame_count)+3; unpauses. Frames below last are recorded. At frame >= last, should_finish_recording is True, and finish_recording releases the writer in the camera process and publishes RecordingFinishedMessage with the list of per-frame metadata (pickled through a multiprocessing.Queue; metadata only, no images).

Timestamps and checks happen after the recording, in the main process. finalize_recording waits for one RecordingFinishedMessage per camera. RecordingFinalizer then writes the per-camera '<rec>.camera<id>.timestamps.csv' files and '<rec>_timestamps.csv' from the metadata lists. validate_recording re-opens each video with cv2 and raises if frame counts differ between cameras or from the timestamp row counts. This catches drops after the fact; it does not prevent them.

The main (FastAPI/uvicorn) process owns the SHM: it creates it with read_only=True and publishes the DTO. Each camera process re-attaches with read_only=False and is the only writer. The main-process handle can only use the non-consuming reads.

The SkellyCam UI reader is the _frontend_image_relay asyncio task inside the websocket handler on the main process event loop. Every 10 ms it checks that the UI has acknowledged the last sent frame (last_received_frontend_confirmation >= last_sent_frame_number). If so, it calls CameraGroupManager.get_latest_frontend_payloads, then send_bytes. After a period of back-pressure it skips one extra cycle.

The acknowledgement comes from the skellycam-ui renderer. It sends {type:'frameAcknowledgment', frameNumber:max} after dispatching decoded bitmaps. The server stores data['frameNumber'] and data.get('displayImageSizes'). skellycam-ui never sends displayImageSizes (grep of skellycam-ui/src finds no match), so the server always applies its default 0.5 scale.

The UI reader reads the 'latest complete' multiframe: target = min over cameras of last_written_index, then get_data_by_index(target) for each camera into per-group recarrays that are reused across calls (probe line 26: True). It raises ValueError if the cameras' frame_numbers differ.

The UI reader can resend duplicates. get_latest_frontend_payload accepts if_newer_than but never uses it. Once the UI has acknowledged, the relay re-reads, re-resizes, re-JPEG-encodes and re-sends the same multiframe whenever no new frame has arrived within 10 ms.

A UI read failure can end a recording. CameraGroupIPC.should_continue includes the global kill flag, so every camera loop exits. Recording is finalized in each loop's finally block, but the session stops.

risks_for_priorities.risk: The disk writer is synchronous in the grab loop, so encoder stalls slow the capture loop rather than filling a buffer. With DSHOW CAP_PROP_BUFFERSIZE=1, the driver silently discards sensor frames the loop did not grab in time. frame_number is a software counter, so these losses are invisible to the writer's consecutive-frame check and to validate_recording (all cameras stay equal). Only grab timestamps reveal them.

Any unhandled exception in the UI image relay sets global_kill_flag, including the ValueError get_latest_multiframe raises on a cross-camera frame-number mismatch. That stops every camera loop and ends an in-progress recording. The file is finalized in the finally block, but the capture is cut short.

The start-recording handshake has a 3-frame margin. If a camera has not dequeued RecordingInfoMessage (multiprocessing.Queue) and built its VideoRecorder (which includes a codec probe that writes a temp file) before reaching first_recording_frame_number, it raises RuntimeError and the whole app is killed.

Drop detection is only post-hoc. validate_recording compares video frame counts and timestamp rows after the recording, and the writer has no ring or queue of its own to absorb encoder jitter. If the design moves the recorder onto ring reads, the current non-consuming, overwrite=True ring offers no back-pressure or lap detection beyond a pre-copy index check (no seqlock).

Lockstep plus a synchronous encode means the slowest camera's write() sets the frame period for all cameras. Measured with 5 concurrent X264 (MSMF) writers: 1080p write() p99 12.7-13.9 ms, max 23.3 ms; 720p p99 9.9-11.4 ms. The 60 fps budget is 16.7 ms and must also cover retrieve() MJPEG decode, putText and 2 SHM copies, so 5x1080p60 is at risk.

The UI payload is built synchronously on the main asyncio loop: 4.0 ms (720p) and 8.5 ms (1080p) per 5-camera payload. If-newer-than is ignored, so unchanged frames are re-encoded, and the work blocks HTTP control handlers (start/stop recording) on the same loop.

get_images_by_frame_number, used by FreeMoCap's UI path, allocates 5 full-frame recarrays per call because of the never-populated cache: 2.7 ms (720p) and 5.6 ms (1080p), vs 0.8 and 1.9 ms with reuse.

Readers that lag (the FreeMoCap nodes) have only 172 slots (2.87 s at 60 fps) at 1080p before a silent overwrite. On a mismatch they only log a warning and use whatever frame is in the slot, and a torn read is possible because nothing is re-checked after the copy.

Every SHM reader copies whole frames out (np.copyto) instead of using views. That is 1 full copy per camera per UI payload and per FreeMoCap node read, plus a full-payload bytearray slice copy and a JPEG tobytes copy. On the same camera thread as the recorder, the producer makes 2 full copies per frame.
Rotation (when configured) costs one extra full-frame cv2.rotate copy in each consumer independently: the recorder, the UI payload and each FreeMoCap node.

A frame_number that matches after the copy therefore does not prove the image bytes are consistent. This is structural inference; no torn read was reproduced.

The disk writer (VideoRecorder) does not read from the ring buffer. In the camera loop, put_frame(frame_rec_array) (line 96) is followed directly by handle_video_recording(frame_rec_array=...) (lines 99-105). That calls video_recorder.record_frame(frame=frame_rec_array) (handle_video_recording_loop.py:24) on the camera process's own local recarray, not on the SHM slot. Probe: frame.image[0] shares memory with the local recarray and not with the SHM ring.

The recorder runs inside the camera worker. Standalone SkellyCam creates its WorkerRegistry with WorkerMode.PROCESS (__main__.py:39-43), and FreeMoCap's __main__.py:57-61 does the same, so each camera is a multiprocessing.Process (managed_worker.py:239). There is no recorder thread, queue or process. Encoding runs synchronously in the grab loop, with one VideoRecorder per camera.

VideoRecorder.create resolves a fourcc with resolve_writer_fourcc. It tries the requested fourcc first (default 'X264', camera_config.py:29), then WEB_COMPATIBLE_CODECS [X264, H264, avc1, X264_PYAV], then NON_WEB_CODECS [mp4v, XVID, MJPG]. It then opens either cv2.VideoWriter(path, fourcc, framerate, (w,h)) or PyavVideoWriter (libx264, yuv420p, crf 18, preset fast). The extension comes from FOURCC_TO_EXTENSION: mp4 for X264/H264/avc1/X264_PYAV/mp4v, avi for XVID/DIVX/MJPG. The framerate passed is the camera loop's median over its last 1000 loop intervals, once at least 30 exist. That interval runs from the end of the previous iteration (line 117) to just after retrieve (line 80), so it leaves out this camera's own put_frame and record time and is not a true frame period. When fewer than 30 intervals exist, config.framerate is used, and its default is -1.0.

On this machine (opencv 4.12.0, SkellyCam venv), cv2.VideoWriter with 'X264', 'H264' or 'avc1' opens on the MSMF (Media Foundation) backend. FFmpeg first remaps the tag to avc1 and tries libopenh264, which fails to load (openh264-1.8.0-win64.dll, 'Incorrect library version loaded'). 'MJPG' opens on FFMPEG. _probe_codec('X264') therefore succeeds via MSMF, and the default disk writer here is the Media Foundation H.264 encoder. Whether that MFT is hardware (NVENC) or software is not established.

record_frame hands the encoder frame.image[0], which is a C-contiguous view of the local recarray, not a copy. It allocates a new rotated image with cv2.rotate only when camera_info.rotation != -1 (lines 92-98). Its only other explicit copy is copy(frame.frame_metadata) at line 108: 632 B of metadata (FRAME_METADATA_DTYPE.itemsize), which does not share memory with the frame, appended to an in-memory list on every frame.

The writer detects gaps with _validate_frame_number, which raises ValueError if a frame is not previous+1. The exception propagates to the camera loop's except block, which calls ipc.kill_everything() (global_kill_flag=True). The finally block still calls finish_recording, because video_recorder still holds the pre-exception recorder, so the file is released. frame_number is a software counter that increments per successful retrieve, so this check cannot see frames the camera or driver dropped upstream.

On Windows the capture is opened on DSHOW (determine_backend.py:29-42), and the code REQUESTS CAP_PROP_BUFFERSIZE=1 (create_cv2_video_capture.py:62). If the backend rejects that, it only logs at debug level (lines 62-66). The code comments say DSHOW honours the setting and MSMF ignores it (line 27), but that has not been verified on the target cameras. If the loop, including the synchronous encode, runs slower than the sensor, frames the loop never grabbed leave no counter anywhere in SkellyCam (inference). The only trace would be the spacing of the per-frame grab timestamps. ServerFramerateCalculator explicitly assumes frame_number increments once per hardware capture (websocket_server.py:38-44), and that assumption fails under driver-side drops.

The recorder throttles all cameras, not only its own. should_grab_by_id lets a camera grab only when its frame_count <= every other camera's frame_count (lockstep, camera_orchestrator.py:96-109). frame_count is updated at opencv_camera_loop.py:116, after handle_video_recording and check_framerate_reset have returned. One camera's slow write() therefore delays the next grab of every camera.

Measured write() cost of the default 'X264' path (MSMF here) on synthetic frames: gradient, moving box and noise, 60 distinct frames cycled, 300 frames per writer, free-running, not lockstepped, no capture load. One writer: 720p median 0.55 ms, p99 1.32 ms; 1080p median 0.88 ms, p99 1.73 ms. Five concurrent writer processes: 720p median 1.02-2.01 ms, p99 9.86-11.35 ms, max 15.44 ms; 1080p median 3.92-4.69 ms, p99 12.67-13.91 ms, max 23.28 ms. release() takes 0.30-0.54 s with one writer and 0.42-1.15 s with five, which suggests write() returns before encoding finishes (inference). Sustained rate per writer with five writers, measured from first write through release: 270-325 fps at 720p and 118-122 fps at 1080p.

claim_verdicts.final_statement: Recording start is applied by frame number. start_recording does this in order: pause all cameras and wait; set last_recording_frame_number=-1 and first_recording_frame_number=max(frame_count)+3; publish RecordingInfoMessage; start the AudioRecorder if a mic is selected; await 10 ms; unpause and wait. should_record_frame_number returns True when first != -1 and frame_number >= first.

Each camera builds its VideoRecorder in its own process when it dequeues RecordingInfoMessage from its own multiprocessing.Queue subscription. This happens in check_for_new_recording_info, called from camera_loop_update_checks before the pause check, so it also runs while paused. Creation includes _probe_codec, which opens a cv2.VideoWriter on a temp file, writes one frame, releases it and checks the file. On win32 the probe timeout is not armed. The camera then busy-waits until all cameras report recording_in_progress. If the message has not been consumed by the time the camera reaches first_recording_frame_number, handle_video_recording raises RuntimeError('Record requested before video_recorder was created'). That kills the session; it is not a silent drop.

Recording stop is also frame-number based. stop_recording pauses and waits, stops audio, sets first=-1 and last=max(frame_count)+3, then unpauses. Frames below last are recorded. At frame >= last, should_finish_recording is True and finish_recording runs in the camera process: it releases the writer and publishes RecordingFinishedMessage with the list of per-frame metadata, pickled through a multiprocessing.Queue (metadata only, no images).

Timestamps and checks happen after the recording, in the main process. finalize_recording polls every 100 ms for one RecordingFinishedMessage per camera while ipc.should_continue holds, and raises if any message is missing. RecordingFinalizer then validates the metadata lists: equal counts and equal frame numbers across cameras (validate_frame_metadatas, lines 21-69). It writes the per-camera timestamp CSVs and the multiframe CSV (process_and_save_recording_timestamps, lines 72-115). validate_recording then re-opens each video with cv2. It raises if CAP_PROP_FRAME_COUNT differs between cameras, or from the CSV row count, which it reads with polars. This catches drops after the fact; it does not prevent them.

The SkellyCam UI reader is the _frontend_image_relay asyncio task, one of four tasks created in WebsocketServer.run on the main-process event loop. Each cycle it awaits 10 ms, then checks that the UI has acknowledged the last sent frame (last_received_frontend_confirmation >= last_sent_frame_number). If so, it calls CameraGroupManager.get_latest_frontend_payloads, which builds the payloads for ALL camera groups first, and then calls send_bytes for each. A cycle that finds the ack missing sets skipped_previous, and the next acknowledged cycle is skipped as well. last_sent_frame_number is one value shared by all camera groups.

A UI read failure can end a recording. Any exception in _frontend_image_relay other than WebSocketDisconnect, AssertionError, CancelledError or a RuntimeError containing 'close' sets global_kill_flag=True. The websocket's app.state.global_kill_flag is the same flag the CameraGroupManager passes to CameraGroupIPC, and CameraGroupIPC.should_continue includes it, so every camera loop exits. Each loop's finally block releases its writer, but the session stops.

A grab-failure fall-through desynchronizes ring index from frame_number. If 30 consecutive opencv_get_frame attempts fail while the capture is still open, the retry loop exits with frame_success False, and nothing checks it. The stale frame is put into SHM at a new ring index with an unchanged frame_number (lines 72-96). Then: (a) get_latest_multiframe compares frame_numbers at the same ring index across cameras, finds a mismatch and raises ValueError; the UI relay turns that into global_kill_flag. (b) If recording, the same frame_number reaches record_frame twice and _validate_frame_number raises, which kills the session. This is a concrete trigger for the R26 path.

stop_recording pauses capture in the MIDDLE of a recording. It pauses and waits for all cameras, stops the AudioRecorder, sets last=max(frame_count)+3, then unpauses. No frames are grabbed during that window, but frame_number does not jump. The recording therefore contains a silent time gap before its final 3 frames or fewer. It passes every consecutive-frame check and validate_recording, and is visible only in the grab timestamps (inference from code; the gap length was not measured).

check_framerate_reset can release and recreate the cv2.VideoCapture in the middle of a recording. Past frame 100, if more than 30 consecutive loop intervals exceed 2x a HARD-CODED 30 fps period (66.7 ms), it reopens the camera, and create_cv2_video_capture can wait_1s per retry. This runs before frame_count is updated (line 116), so the reopen stalls every camera through lockstep. No frames are numbered during the stall, so the gap is silent. The threshold ignores the configured framerate.

Every frame, including every frame written to disk, has a text stamp ('camera.id..idx..fr..') burned into its pixels by two cv2.putText calls before put_frame and record_frame. The recorded videos and the FreeMoCap inputs therefore carry the overlay. This is not a copy, but it modifies the data on the disk path and adds per-frame CPU.

Timestamp CSVs are written only via stop_recording -> finalize_recording. That function loops only while ipc.should_continue and raises 'Not all cameras finished recording successfully' if any camera's message is missing. After a global kill (R13, R26), each camera releases its video file in its finally block, but the main process does not produce the timestamp CSVs and validation does not run. Separately, validate_recording imports polars inside a try (line 192), so in the SkellyCam .venv, where polars is missing, check 4 raises ValueError and every finalize would fail.

The ring's overwrite protection cannot be enabled with the current readers. No reader advances last_read_index, so it stays at -1. _check_for_overwrite is then true at every index with index % L == L-1, so put_data(overwrite_allowed=False) would raise on the first wrap even with no reader behind. Making the disk writer a protected ring consumer would need a real per-consumer read cursor, and a reader that holds a slot by view would need a slot-release protocol.

read_only on SHM handles is not enforced at the memory level. The numpy view of the ring is writeable even on a read_only=True handle (flags.writeable=True), so any reader process can scribble over frames that the recorder or other readers will consume.

The start-recording race (R18) is narrower than the mapper's P1 risk implies. A camera that dequeues RecordingInfoMessage sets recording_in_progress and busy-waits until every camera is recording, without advancing its frame_count. Through lockstep, the other cameras can then get at most one frame ahead of it, which is below first = max+3. RuntimeError therefore needs EVERY camera's queue to still be empty when it reaches first. Messages are published while the cameras are paused, and paused cameras poll the queue every 1 ms. This is inference; it was not reproduced.

Per-frame metadata accumulates in memory for the whole recording and is shipped once, at the end, in a single pickled multiprocessing.Queue message per camera. At 632 B/frame that is about 136 MB per camera per hour at 60 fps (about 680 MB for 5 cameras) before numpy object overhead. A long recording risks a large stall or a memory spike at stop. It also means no timestamps survive a crash (see the finalize item above).

risk_verdicts.risk: The disk writer is synchronous in the grab loop, so encoder stalls slow the capture loop instead of filling a buffer. Sensor frames the loop does not grab in time leave no counter anywhere in SkellyCam. DSHOW honouring CAP_PROP_BUFFERSIZE=1 is requested but unverified. frame_number is a software counter, so these losses are invisible to the writer's consecutive-frame check and to validate_recording, where all cameras stay equal. The same is true of the stop_recording pause and a check_framerate_reset reopen in the middle of a recording. Only grab timestamps reveal them.

Any unhandled exception in the UI image relay sets global_kill_flag. That includes the ValueError get_latest_multiframe raises on a cross-camera frame-number mismatch, which the 30-failure grab fall-through can trigger. Every camera loop stops and an in-progress recording ends. Video files are released in each loop's finally block, but finalize_recording, which writes the timestamp CSVs, never completes.

The start-recording handshake has a 3-frame margin. A camera that reaches first_recording_frame_number without having built its VideoRecorder raises RuntimeError, which kills the app. This needs every camera's mp.Queue to still be empty when it reaches that frame. Once any camera dequeues, it busy-waits and lockstep holds the others within about one frame of it. The risk is real but low-probability, and it was not reproduced.

Drop detection is only post-hoc: validate_recording compares video frame counts and timestamp rows after the recording ends. The writer has no ring or queue of its own to absorb encoder jitter. If the recorder were moved onto ring reads, the current ring would not protect it. Its readers do not consume and it writes with overwrite=True, so it offers no back-pressure. Its overwrite guard cannot be enabled while last_read_index stays at -1, and lap detection is a single pre-copy index check (no seqlock).

Lockstep plus a synchronous encode means the slowest camera's put_frame and write() set the frame period for all cameras. Measured with 5 concurrent free-running X264 (MSMF) writers: write() p99 is 12.7-13.9 ms (max 23.3 ms) at 1080p and 9.9-11.4 ms at 720p. put_frame adds 1.5-2.4 ms at 1080p, measured separately. The 60 fps budget is 16.7 ms and must also cover retrieve() (MJPEG decode) and 2x putText, so 5x1080p60 is at risk.

The UI payload is built synchronously on the main asyncio loop: 4.0 ms (720p) and 8.5 ms (1080p) per 5-camera payload. if_newer_than is ignored, so unchanged frames are re-copied and re-encoded. The work blocks the other coroutines on that loop, including the async start and stop recording handlers. Those handlers pause the cameras anyway, so this delays control rather than dropping recorded frames.

get_images_by_frame_number, used by FreeMoCap's UI path, allocates 5 full-frame recarrays per call because its cache is never populated: 2.7 ms (720p) and 5.6 ms (1080p), against 0.8 and 1.9 ms with reuse.

Lagging readers (the FreeMoCap nodes) get only 172 slots (2.87 s at 1080p60) before a silent overwrite. A reader near the tail has about one frame period before its slot is rewritten. On a frame-number mismatch the nodes only log a warning and use whatever frame is in the slot. A torn read (frame_number matches, image partly new) is possible because nothing is re-checked after the copy (inference, not reproduced).

Every SHM reader copies whole frames out with np.copyto instead of using views: 1 full copy per camera per UI payload and per FreeMoCap node read. On top of that come a full-payload bytearray slice copy and a JPEG tobytes copy. The memoryview fix for the slice copy is unsafe with the current shared global buffer. On the recorder's thread, the producer makes 2 full copies per frame and takes a slow assignment path.
Rotation, when configured, costs an extra full-frame cv2.rotate in each consumer independently: the recorder, the UI payload and each FreeMoCap node.

map.summary: SkellyCam's control plane runs on two transports. (1) A home-made pub/sub in which every subscription is its own multiprocessing.Queue. Subscriptions are created in the main process and pickled into each camera process when it is spawned. It carries config requests, extracted configs, the shared-memory DTO, recording start info and recording-finished metadata. (2) Many lock-protected multiprocessing.Value flags (should_pause, should_close, is_paused, updating, frame_count, first/last_recording_frame_number, global kill, group shutdown, heartbeat). These handle pause/close/kill and frame-by-frame lockstep sync. Every command comes from an HTTP endpoint (FastAPI, main process). The websocket carries only frame acknowledgements, ping and server-to-UI telemetry. Each camera process checks all control inputs inside its single capture loop at the top of every iteration (non-blocking Queue.empty() checks plus Value reads). Applying a config update, opening a VideoRecorder and closing/finalising a recording all run synchronously in that loop. Video encoding (record_frame) also runs in that loop, before frame_count is incremented. Because of the lockstep orchestrator, the slowest camera's capture + shared-memory copy + encode therefore sets the frame period for every camera. Measured on this machine: the per-iteration control poll costs about 41 us with 5 cameras, but the 'wait_10us' back-off really sleeps about 0.52 ms (median). For the ring/IPC code there is no difference between 23ccbf20 and the 777b058c that FreeMoCap runs: the trees are identical.

claims.statement: PubSub transport: each PubSubTopicABC holds a list of multiprocessing.Queue objects, one per subscriber. get_subscription() refuses to run outside the main process. publish() type-checks the message and then calls sub.put(message) on every subscriber queue, so each message is pickled once per subscriber. With overwrite=True it first drains the queue with a get() loop. A publish with zero subscribers is dropped with a warning.

There are 7 topics: UPDATE_CAMERA_SETTINGS, EXTRACTED_CONFIG, SHM_UPDATES, RECORDING_INFO, RECORDING_FINISHED, FRAMERATE, LOGS. One PubSubTopicManager is created per camera group, only in the main process, and kept in the global dict CAMERA_GROUP_PUB_SUB_MANAGERS.

Message payloads: UpdateCamerasSettingsMessage(requested_configs), DeviceExtractedConfigMessage(extracted_config), SetShmMessage(CameraGroupSharedMemoryDTO, which holds shm names, dtype and shape only, no pixels), RecordingInfoMessage(recording_info), RecordingFinishedMessage(recording_info, frame_metadatas: list[np.recarray]), FramerateMessage. The control plane never carries image pixels.

Wiring: CameraGroupIPC.create subscribes the main process to EXTRACTED_CONFIG and RECORDING_FINISHED. CameraManager.create makes one subscription per camera for UPDATE_CAMERA_SETTINGS, SHM_UPDATES and RECORDING_INFO and passes those queues, together with the whole ipc object (including the PubSubTopicManager and its queue lists), as kwargs to the camera worker. The kwargs are pickled into the child at Process.start() (spawn), so a subscription added after start would not reach an already running child's copy of the topic.

FRAMERATE is subscribed (CameraGroupManager) but never published anywhere in skellycam (grep finds publish() calls only for EXTRACTED_CONFIG, RECORDING_FINISHED, UPDATE_CAMERA_SETTINGS, RECORDING_INFO, SHM_UPDATES). So get_backend_framerate_updates() always returns {}. The framerate the UI sees is computed in the websocket relay instead.

Shared control flags are multiprocessing.Value with the default lock=True. CameraStatus has 11 bool flags plus frame_count. CameraGroupIPC has should_pause and shutdown_camera_group_flag, plus global_kill_flag and heartbeat_timestamp passed in. CameraOrchestrator has first/last_recording_frame_number. Measured: a lock=True .value read costs 306 ns versus 35 ns for RawValue (benchmark line A).

ipc.should_continue = not shutdown_camera_group_flag AND not global_kill_flag AND heartbeat fresh (3 locked reads plus perf_counter; measured 2.8 us, benchmark line B). The heartbeat is written once per second by a WorkerRegistry thread. Children only declare the parent dead after 300 s without one.

Per-frame control polling: every iteration of the camera loop first runs camera_loop_update_checks, which does a non-blocking empty() check on the RECORDING_INFO queue, then on the UPDATE_CAMERA_SETTINGS queue, then reconciles should_pause and is_paused. The loop then checks should_close and is_paused (if paused it sleeps wait_1ms and continues), then orchestrator.should_grab_by_id (if false it sleeps wait_10us and continues). Every control input is therefore handled in the same thread as frame capture. There is no separate control thread in the camera process.

Measured cost of that poll with 5 cameras, idle queues, main process, no cross-process contention: mp.Queue.empty() 8.9 us each, camera_loop_update_checks 18.0 us, should_grab_by_id 18.4 us, full pre-grab poll 40.9 us. The back-off sleeps are much longer than their names say: time.sleep(1e-5) ('wait_10us') has a median of 523.5 us (p99 1002.5 us), and wait_1ms has a median of 1531 us. So after the slowest camera bumps frame_count, the waiting cameras wake on average about 0.5 ms late. Results are in C:/Users/Dom/AppData/Local/Temp/claude/c--Users-Dom-GitHub-freemocap-skellycam/ad23e4da-d956-400c-b95c-1c7166f96ad9/scratchpad/control_plane/bench_control_plane_results.txt. Note: the script prints all results and then hangs at interpreter exit, so run it with a timeout.

Lockstep sync is a control signal read every frame. should_grab_by_id returns False unless all cameras are 'ready' (7 locked flags each) and this camera's frame_count <= every other camera's frame_count. A camera only bumps its frame_count after put_frame, handle_video_recording (encode) and check_framerate_reset. So the next grab for all cameras waits for the slowest camera's whole grab+retrieve+shm copy+encode.

Video encoding runs synchronously in the camera capture loop. handle_video_recording calls VideoRecorder.record_frame, which calls video_writer.write(image) (cv2.VideoWriter or PyAV libx264), on the process-local frame_rec_array right after it is copied into shm. The recorder never reads from the shared-memory ring.

Because recording does not consume the ring, ring overwrites cannot cause disk-write drops. The camera writes with overwrite=True. Nothing in skellycam calls get_next_data/retrieve_next_frame or advances last_read_index (grep outside the ring classes and tests finds no hits). Recorded frames are additionally checked for consecutive frame numbers, and a gap raises.

Start-recording command: POST /skellycam/camera/group/all/record/start -> CameraGroupManager.start_recording_all_groups -> CameraGroup.start_recording. Steps: (a) set should_pause on every camera and await all is_paused (10 ms asyncio polls); (b) last_recording_frame_number=-1, first_recording_frame_number=max(frame_count)+3; (c) publish RecordingInfoMessage; (d) optionally start the AudioRecorder; (e) sleep 10 ms, then unpause and await.

On the camera side, RecordingInfoMessage is picked up by check_for_new_recording_info. This runs before the pause check, so it also runs while paused. It builds the VideoRecorder inline (resolve_writer_fourcc probes codecs and opens the file), sets recording_in_progress, then busy-waits in wait_1ms (real about 1.5 ms) until every camera is recording. There is no timeout apart from ipc.should_continue. While a camera sits in that wait its is_paused stays True, so the orchestrator's unpause await cannot finish until all cameras have a recorder. Combined with the frame_count lockstep, a late camera can be at most 1 frame ahead, which stays under the +3 frame start margin.

Each frame, whether to record and where to stop is decided by comparing the frame number with the two shared Values: record if frame >= first (when first != -1), or if frame < last (when last != -1); finish when frame >= last. These flags are read before grabbing_frame is cleared, so all cameras see a consistent decision.

Stop-recording command: GET /skellycam/camera/group/all/record/stop -> CameraGroup.stop_recording. It pauses and awaits, stops audio, sets first=-1 and last=max(frame_count)+3, unpauses, then finalize_recording polls recording_finished_subscription every 100 ms with no timeout (only ipc.should_continue) until every camera has sent RecordingFinishedMessage. It then runs RecordingFinalizer.

Finishing a recording runs inside the camera frame loop. finish_recording calls video_writer.release() (flush) and builds RecordingFinishedMessage, whose __post_init__ walks every frame's metadata to check sequential numbering, then puts it on the queue. Measured for 36,000 frames (10 min at 60 fps): __post_init__ 387 ms, pickle 127 ms, 23.9 MB per camera, unpickle 98 ms (benchmark line G; FRAME_METADATA_DTYPE itemsize is 632 B). The main process unpickles it on its asyncio thread via a blocking get().

Config-update command: POST /skellycam/camera/group/apply. For an existing group this publishes UpdateCamerasSettingsMessage to every camera and awaits EXTRACTED_CONFIG replies, polling every 100 ms. In the camera, check_for_new_config (inside the frame loop, not paused) sets updating=True and applies cv2 properties synchronously. With exposure_mode RECOMMEND that means 9 exposure steps x 11 cap.read() calls. It then patches the per-frame camera_info, publishes the extracted config and clears updating. While updating is True, orchestrator.all_ready is False, so every camera in the group stops grabbing.

A config update does not reallocate the process-local frame_rec_array (its dtype is fixed by create_frame_dtype from the original resolution) or the shm ring. Nothing stops an update from arriving while a recording is in progress.

Connect/startup handshake: CameraGroup.start spawns the workers, staggered 0.25 s each on Windows with time.sleep inside the async call. Each worker opens cv2, publishes DeviceExtractedConfigMessage, then polls shm_subscription every 10 ms. The main process awaits all extracted configs, creates CameraGroupSharedMemory from the extracted configs (its own handle is read_only=True), and publishes SetShmMessage once. Each camera recreates its ring with read_only=False, sets connected, and drains frames with cap.read() until all_ready.

Pause/unpause command: GET /skellycam/camera/group/all/pause_unpause toggles per-camera should_pause and awaits the cameras' is_paused acknowledgement. CameraGroupManager.pause_all_groups and unpause_all_groups call camera_group.pause and camera_group.unpause, but CameraGroup has no such methods (only pause_unpause), so that code would raise AttributeError. Only tests mock it.

Close command: DELETE /skellycam/camera/group/close/all -> CameraGroup.close. It stops any active recording first, sets shutdown_camera_group_flag, then CameraManager.close sets should_close on every camera and spins with time.sleep(0.1) until all report closed. It then joins / terminates / kills with 3+3+2 s timeouts. All of this is synchronous on the FastAPI asyncio thread. Finally the shm is unlinked.

Shutdown command: GET /shutdown sets global_kill_flag, sleeps 100 ms and sends SIGTERM to its own process. The handler sets server.should_exit, and main()'s finally calls WorkerRegistry.shutdown_all (kill flag -> join 3 s -> terminate -> kill). The registry's child-monitor thread also SIGTERMs the parent if any worker dies with a non-zero exit code or if anyone sets global_kill_flag.

Failure escalation is app-wide. Any exception in the camera loop calls ipc.kill_everything() (global_kill_flag=True). Any camera worker exit also sets shutdown_camera_group_flag in its finally block. ManagedProcess sets global_kill_flag on unhandled exceptions and on SIGTERM/SIGINT. The websocket tasks set global_kill_flag on unexpected errors.

Grab-failure path: the retry loop exits once fail_count reaches MAX_FAIL_COUNT=30 even if frame_success is still False. The code does not check frame_success after the loop. It still calls put_frame and handle_video_recording with a frame whose frame_number was not incremented (the increment only happens on success). For a recording camera, _validate_frame_number then raises, which leads to kill_everything.

check_framerate_reset is a self-triggered control action inside the frame loop. It hardcodes a 30 fps target, so the limit is 2 x 33.3 ms = 66.7 ms measured from post-grab to after the record step. After frame 100, if that limit is exceeded for more than 30 consecutive frames, it releases and re-creates the cv2.VideoCapture inline. There is no recording guard, and the new config is not republished.

The websocket (/skellycam/websocket/connect) does not carry commands. Client to server: only JSON {frameNumber, displayImageSizes} acknowledgements, plus ping/pong. Server to client: binary frame payloads (relay polls shm every 10 ms and sends only when the last frame has been acknowledged), framerate_update (about 4 Hz), app_state (when changed, checked every 1 s) and log records. skellycam-ui sends {type:'frameAcknowledgment', frameNumber} and never sends displayImageSizes (grep for displayImageSize in skellycam-ui/src finds nothing). On every ack the server overwrites _display_image_sizes with data.get('displayImageSizes', None).

UI endpoint map: skellycam-ui calls /shutdown, /skellycam/camera/group/apply, /group/close/all, /group/all/record/start, /group/all/record/stop and /group/all/pause_unpause. It also defines updateConfigs=/skellycam/camera/update, which has no matching route in camera_router (that router defines detect, microphone/detect, group/apply, record/start, record/stop, close/all, pause_unpause).

Metadata that travels with each frame lives inside the same shm ring slot as the pixels: frame_metadata = camera_info (camera_id U128, camera_index, rotation, color_channels), frame_number, timebase_mapping, and 9 lifecycle timestamps (632 B total). The ring write index doubles as the frame number: latest_frame_number returns last_written_index, and readers index the ring by frame number.

Timestamp ordering means shm readers (UI, FreeMoCap) never see the later lifecycle stamps. pre_copy_to_camera_shm_ns is set before put_frame, but post_copy_to_camera_shm_ns and pre/post_frame_record_ns are set after the frame has been copied into shm. They are then reset to 0 for the next frame. Only the recorder's per-frame metadata copy, taken after write, contains all 9 timestamps.

Camera configs move as follows. Requested config: HTTP body -> pickled into the worker kwargs at spawn. Actual config: EXTRACTED_CONFIG queue. Full configs for readers: inside CameraGroupSharedMemoryDTO via SetShmMessage. Slim per-frame camera_info: inside every ring slot. The writer fps used by VideoRecorder is the camera loop's measured median framerate over the last up to 1000 frame intervals, passed in at recorder creation.

beartype_this_package() is enabled in skellycam/__init__.py. Every annotated function in the package, including the per-frame camera-loop helpers, is wrapped with runtime type checks. Confirmed by a BeartypeCallHintParamViolation raised from camera_loop_update_checks and from PubSubTopicManager.get_subscription, recorded in the pytest output C:/Users/Dom/AppData/Local/Temp/claude/c--Users-Dom-GitHub-freemocap-skellycam/ad23e4da-d956-400c-b95c-1c7166f96ad9/scratchpad/control_plane/pytest_control_plane.txt (43 passed, 1 failed because beartype raises before the expected ValueError).

Child-process logs go to the skellylogs websocket queue: a multiprocessing.Queue with maxsize 1000, written with put_nowait, and records are silently dropped when it is full. Logging therefore cannot block the camera loop. The main-process _logs_relay drains it only while a websocket client is connected. The skellylogs package is not in either repo; it lives at C:/Users/Dom/GitHub/freemocap/skellycam/.venv/Lib/site-packages/skellylogs/handlers/websocket_log_queue_handler.py, lines 106-112, 179-181 and 186-194.

frame_copies.where: Camera process, SharedMemoryRingBuffer.put_data via put_frame, every frame
frame_copies.necessary: copy(data) makes a temporary full-frame copy, then assigning it into the ring slot copies again. Only the slot write is needed. Measured at 1080p BGR (6.22 MB): put_data 1.680 ms, copy(frame) alone 0.971 ms, a single np.copyto into the slot 0.206 ms (benchmark line H in C:/Users/Dom/AppData/Local/Temp/claude/c--Users-Dom-GitHub-freemocap-skellycam/ad23e4da-d956-400c-b95c-1c7166f96ad9/scratchpad/control_plane/bench_control_plane_results.txt). One copy is avoidable, and because of the lockstep the cost lands on every camera's frame period.

frame_copies.where: Camera process, cap.retrieve(image=frame_rec_array.image[0])
frame_copies.kind: decode (MJPEG/raw to BGR) into a preallocated buffer
frame_copies.necessary: This is the materialisation of the frame from the driver. The decode target is preallocated, so there is no extra Python-side copy. It could only be avoided by recording the compressed stream directly.

frame_copies.where: Camera process, VideoRecorder.record_frame rotation
frame_copies.kind: numpy copy (cv2.rotate allocates a new image)
frame_copies.necessary: Only happens when camera_info.rotation != -1. It could be avoided with container rotation metadata or by rotating at read time.

frame_copies.where: Camera process, video_writer.write (cv2.VideoWriter), or PyavVideoWriter.write (av.VideoFrame.from_ndarray, then bgr24 to yuv420p, then libx264 encode)
frame_copies.kind: encode (plus a copy into an AVFrame on the PyAV path)
frame_copies.necessary: The encode is required for the disk write. It runs synchronously in the capture loop, so it is on the critical path for the whole lockstep group.

frame_copies.where: Camera process, per-frame metadata copy kept by VideoRecorder (metadata only, NOT the image)
frame_copies.necessary: Collected for the timestamps CSV and later pickled into RecordingFinishedMessage (23.9 MB for 36,000 frames). Not an image copy. Listed so the control-plane payload size is on record.

frame_copies.where: Main process, websocket relay -> CameraGroupSharedMemory.get_latest_multiframe -> get_data_by_index, once per websocket send (polled every 10 ms, sent only after the frontend ack)
frame_copies.kind: numpy copy (np.copyto of each camera's full slot into a cached recarray)
frame_copies.necessary: Copies all N full frames out of shm before building the frontend payload. Reading a view and checking frame_number before and after would avoid this copy. Downstream payload encoding belongs to the UI-path area.

frame_copies.where: Camera process, startup only: cap.read() in a loop until all_ready, and in RECOMMEND exposure (99 reads during a config update)
frame_copies.necessary: Clears driver buffers or samples brightness. Not on the steady-state path, but RECOMMEND runs inside the frame loop and stalls the group.

flow_steps.action: HTTP POST /skellycam/camera/group/apply with camera_configs
CameraGroup.create: CameraGroupIPC + PubSubTopicManager, CameraStatus Values, per-camera subscription queues; start() spawns the workers (0.25 s stagger)
Open cv2.VideoCapture, publish DeviceExtractedConfigMessage on the EXTRACTED_CONFIG queue, poll the SHM_UPDATES queue every 10 ms
await_extracted_configs (100 ms polls), create the shm ring per camera, publish SetShmMessage (DTO with shm names)
Recreate the ring read_only=False, set connected=True, drain the driver until all_ready
Each iteration: should_continue -> RECORDING_INFO empty()? -> UPDATE_CAMERA_SETTINGS empty()? -> pause reconcile -> should_close / is_paused -> should_grab_by_id (lockstep on frame_count)

grab/retrieve, read should_record flags, put_frame into the shm ring (overwrite=True), record_frame (encode) if recording, check_framerate_reset, then frame_count = frame_number (releases the lockstep for the others)
flow_steps.to: Shared memory ring / disk / other camera processes via frame_count

flow_steps.action: HTTP POST /skellycam/camera/group/all/record/start
Set should_pause, await is_paused; set first_recording_frame_number=max+3; publish RecordingInfoMessage; start audio; unpause and await
check_for_new_recording_info: build the VideoRecorder (codec probe, open file), recording_in_progress=True, busy-wait until all cameras are recording; frames >= first are written by record_frame
HTTP GET /skellycam/camera/group/all/record/stop
Pause; stop audio; last_recording_frame_number=max+3; unpause; poll the RECORDING_FINISHED queue every 100 ms
At frame >= last: writer.release(), build RecordingFinishedMessage (per-frame metadata list) and put it on the queue
Unpickle the messages, run RecordingFinalizer (timestamps, remux), return stats in the HTTP response
Websocket: send frameAcknowledgment {frameNumber} after rendering
Every 10 ms, if acknowledged, copy the latest multiframe out of shm and send binary; send framerate about 4 Hz and app_state about 1 Hz
HTTP DELETE /skellycam/camera/group/close/all, or GET /shutdown

close: stop recording if active, set shutdown_camera_group_flag and should_close, spin on closed (time.sleep 0.1), join/terminate/kill, unlink shm. shutdown: global_kill_flag + SIGTERM -> WorkerRegistry.shutdown_all
Heartbeat Value written every 1 s; child monitor SIGTERMs the parent on worker crash or when global_kill_flag is set
flow_steps.to: Camera process (reads the heartbeat in should_continue)

risks_for_priorities.risk: Encoding runs inside the capture loop, and frame_count is bumped only after encoding. The lockstep orchestrator then makes every camera's frame period at least the slowest camera's grab+retrieve+shm copy (about 1.7 ms at 1080p, measured)+encode, plus about 0.5 ms average wake-up latency from wait_10us (measured median 523 us). Capture and encode cannot overlap. With 5 x 1080p60 the full chain must stay under about 16.7 ms on the slowest camera.

Every frame-loop iteration does around 40 lock-protected Value reads for 5 cameras (7 ready flags + frame_count per camera in should_grab_by_id), 2 Queue.empty() pipe peeks (8.9 us each) and beartype-wrapped calls. Measured about 41 us per poll without contention. While waiting, 5 processes each spin on the same locks at about 2 kHz; cross-process lock contention was not measured. RawValue reads cost 35 ns versus 306 ns.

A burst of 30 consecutive grab failures exits the retry loop without checking frame_success. The stale, un-incremented frame is then recorded, _validate_frame_number raises, kill_everything runs, and the whole app shuts down mid-recording. The current file is closed in the finally block, but the session ends.

check_framerate_reset hardcodes a 30 fps target. If post-grab-to-post-record time exceeds 66.7 ms for 30 frames in a row (for example a slow encoder at 5x1080p), it releases and reopens the camera inside the loop with no recording guard. This stalls the whole group for the reopen (create_cv2_video_capture retries with 1 s waits) during an active recording.

Config updates (/group/apply on an existing group) are not blocked during recording. They run inline in the frame loop and set updating=True, which halts all cameras (seconds in RECOMMEND exposure mode). If a resolution changes mid-recording, the recorder's shape check raises and the app is killed.

Every failure escalates to the whole app: any camera-loop exception, any websocket task error, or any non-zero worker exit sets global_kill_flag and SIGTERMs the server. A UI or relay bug can therefore end a recording. Separately, finalize_recording and the camera-side all-cameras-recording busy-wait have no timeouts.

Finishing a long recording stalls the camera loop. RecordingFinishedMessage.__post_init__ took 387 ms for 36,000 frames, plus writer.release(), plus 127 ms pickle (feeder thread, same GIL). Because of the lockstep, all cameras freeze. The main asyncio thread then unpickles about 24 MB per camera (98 ms each), which stalls the websocket relay.

put_data copies every frame twice (copy(data) and then the slot assignment): 1.68 ms versus 0.21 ms for a single copyto at 1080p. The main-process UI relay copies all N full frames out of shm on every send.

Main-process control handlers block the asyncio event loop with synchronous sleeps and joins (CameraManager.start 0.25 s per camera, orchestrator.close time.sleep(0.1) spin, joins up to 3+3+2 s). This freezes websocket delivery and other HTTP calls during connect and close. Disk writes are not directly affected.

claim_verdicts.final_statement: PubSub transport: each PubSubTopicABC holds a list of multiprocessing.Queue objects, one per subscriber. get_subscription() raises RuntimeError outside the main process. publish() type-checks the message, drops it with a warning if there are no subscribers, and otherwise calls sub.put(message) on every subscriber queue, so each message is pickled once per subscriber (in that queue's feeder thread). With overwrite=True it first drains the queue with an empty()/get() loop.

There are 7 topics: UPDATE_CAMERA_SETTINGS, EXTRACTED_CONFIG, SHM_UPDATES, RECORDING_INFO, RECORDING_FINISHED, FRAMERATE and LOGS. One PubSubTopicManager is created per camera group, only in the main process (it raises otherwise), and kept in the global dict CAMERA_GROUP_PUB_SUB_MANAGERS. If a manager already exists for the same group id, it is closed and replaced.

Message payloads: UpdateCamerasSettingsMessage(requested_configs), DeviceExtractedConfigMessage(extracted_config), SetShmMessage(CameraGroupSharedMemoryDTO), RecordingInfoMessage(recording_info), RecordingFinishedMessage(recording_info, frame_metadatas: list[np.recarray]) and FramerateMessage(current_framerate). The LOGS topic carries LogRecordModel. CameraGroupSharedMemoryDTO holds per-camera SharedMemoryRingBufferDTOs (shm names, dtype, buffer shape) plus the full CameraConfigs. None of these messages carries image pixels.
claim_verdicts.note: The mapper said the DTO holds 'shm names, dtype and shape only'. It also carries camera_configs (camera_group_shared_memory.py L19-22).

CameraManager.create makes one subscription per camera for UPDATE_CAMERA_SETTINGS, SHM_UPDATES and RECORDING_INFO. It passes those queues, plus the whole ipc object (including the PubSubTopicManager and its queue lists) and the orchestrator, as kwargs to multiprocessing.Process. The child gets its own copy of the topic subscription lists at Process.start(). skellycam never calls set_start_method, so this is spawn plus pickling on Windows and macOS, and fork inheritance on Linux under Python 3.12. Either way, a subscription added after start() does not reach a running child. The FRAMERATE subscription is added after CameraGroup.create but before start(), so it is included.

claim_verdicts.final_statement: The shared control flags are multiprocessing.Value with the default lock=True. CameraStatus has 11 bool flags plus frame_count ('q'). CameraGroupIPC has should_pause and shutdown_camera_group_flag, and receives global_kill_flag and heartbeat_timestamp. CameraOrchestrator has first/last_recording_frame_number. CameraGroupIPC.should_pause is never read or written anywhere (pause is per camera via CameraStatus.should_pause). Measured: a lock=True .value read costs 306 ns, versus 35 ns for RawValue (bench_control_plane_results.txt line A).

ipc.should_continue = not shutdown_camera_group_flag AND not global_kill_flag AND a fresh heartbeat. That is 3 locked reads plus time.perf_counter(), measured at 2.8 us (benchmark line B). A WorkerRegistry thread writes the heartbeat about once per second. Children declare the parent dead, and set global_kill_flag, only after 300 s without a heartbeat.

Per-frame control polling. Each camera-loop iteration first evaluates ipc.should_continue (the while condition), then camera_loop_update_checks. That function checks the RECORDING_INFO queue with a non-blocking empty(), then the UPDATE_CAMERA_SETTINGS queue the same way, then reconciles should_pause with is_paused. The loop then checks should_close (break) and is_paused (if paused, wait_1ms and continue), then orchestrator.should_grab_by_id (if false, wait_10us and continue). Every control input is handled on the same thread as frame capture. The camera process has no separate control thread.

So a waiting camera notices that the slowest camera has bumped frame_count up to about 0.5 ms late (about 1 ms at p99).
