claim_verdicts.final_statement: Lockstep sync is a control signal read every frame. should_grab_by_id returns False unless all cameras are 'ready' and this camera's frame_count is <= every other camera's frame_count. 'ready' means connected and not should_pause, should_close, closing, closed, updating or error: 7 locked reads per camera. They sit in all([...]) list literals, so there is no short-circuit: 35 flag reads plus 5 frame_count reads plus a deepcopy of a dict on every poll with 5 cameras. A camera bumps its frame_count only after put_frame, handle_video_recording (encode), check_framerate_reset and initialize_frame_recarray. So no camera can start frame k+2 until every camera has finished frame k+1 (grab+retrieve+shm copy+encode), and the group's period is at least the slowest camera's full chain.

Video encoding runs synchronously in the camera capture loop. handle_video_recording calls VideoRecorder.record_frame, which calls video_writer.write(image) (cv2.VideoWriter or PyavVideoWriter/libx264). It writes the process-local frame_rec_array right after that array is copied into shm. The recorder never reads from the shared-memory ring.

Recording does not consume the ring, so ring overwrites cannot cause disk-write drops. The camera writes with overwrite=True. Outside the ring classes, tests and the diagnostics script check_shm_speed.py, nothing in skellycam or FreeMoCap calls get_next_data or retrieve_next_frame, or advances last_read_index. Recorded frames are checked for consecutive frame numbers, and a gap raises ValueError. That error is caught by the camera loop and escalates to kill_everything, so the check detects a gap but does not protect the recording. The check also cannot see sensor frames the driver drops before grab (see missed facts).

Start-recording command: POST /skellycam/camera/group/all/record/start -> CameraGroupManager.start_recording_all_groups -> CameraGroup.start_recording. Steps: (a) set should_pause on every camera and await all is_paused, polling every 10 ms with asyncio; (b) set last_recording_frame_number=-1 and first_recording_frame_number=max(frame_count)+3; (c) publish RecordingInfoMessage; (d) start the AudioRecorder if mic_device_index >= 0; (e) await 10 ms, then unpause and await.

On the camera side, check_for_new_recording_info picks up the RecordingInfoMessage. It is the first call in camera_loop_update_checks, so it also runs while the camera is paused. It builds the VideoRecorder inline: resolve_writer_fourcc probes each candidate codec by writing one test frame to a temp file, and then the real file is opened. It then sets recording_in_progress and spins in wait_1ms (about 1.5 ms per sleep, measured) until every camera is recording. There is no timeout other than ipc.should_continue. While a camera spins it never reaches check_camera_should_pause, so its is_paused stays True and the main process's unpause await cannot finish until every camera has a recorder. What guarantees that no frame >= first_recording_frame_number is grabbed before a recorder exists is not the +3 margin: (1) all cameras have acknowledged is_paused, which is set only at the loop top after frame_count was written, before first is computed; (2) no camera can leave the pause until all are recording. Frames max+1 and max+2 are grabbed after the unpause but not recorded.
claim_verdicts.note: The mapper's reasoning that 'a late camera can be at most 1 frame ahead, which stays under the +3 margin' is not the mechanism. The margin is not load-bearing.

claim_verdicts.final_statement: Each frame, the decision to record and to stop comes from comparing the frame number with the two shared Values. A frame is recorded if frame >= first (when first != -1) or frame < last (when last != -1). Recording finishes when frame >= last. The values are read before grabbing_frame is cleared, but nothing ever reads grabbing_frame (it is only written), so that ordering gives no synchronisation. Consistency across cameras comes from the main process setting the thresholds while every camera is paused, and from every camera comparing the same frame numbers under lockstep.

claim_verdicts.final_statement: Stop-recording command: GET /skellycam/camera/group/all/record/stop -> CameraGroup.stop_recording. It pauses and awaits, stops audio, sets first=-1 and last=max(frame_count)+3, and unpauses. finalize_recording then polls recording_finished_subscription every 100 ms, with no timeout other than ipc.should_continue, until every camera has sent a RecordingFinishedMessage. It then runs RecordingFinalizer.

Finishing a recording runs inside the camera frame loop. finish_recording -> finish_and_close -> video_writer.release() (flush), then it builds RecordingFinishedMessage, whose __post_init__ makes several passes over every frame's metadata (type, dtype, camera_id, sequential numbering), and puts it on the queue. The main process unpickles it on its asyncio thread through get(), which it calls after an empty() check.

Config-update command: POST /skellycam/camera/group/apply. For an existing group it publishes UpdateCamerasSettingsMessage to every camera and awaits EXTRACTED_CONFIG replies, polling every 100 ms. In the camera, check_for_new_config runs inside the frame loop, even while paused. It sets updating=True and applies the cv2 properties synchronously: exposure, resolution if changed, and capture fourcc if changed. With exposure_mode RECOMMEND (skipped on Linux, where auto exposure is forced) that is 9 exposure settings x (10 settle + 1 sample) = 99 cap.read() calls. It then patches the per-frame camera_info, publishes the extracted config and clears updating. While updating is True, orchestrator.all_ready is False, so every camera in the group stops grabbing.

A config update reallocates neither the process-local frame_rec_array (its dtype is fixed by create_frame_dtype from the original resolution) nor the shm ring, yet apply_camera_configuration does set new CAP_PROP_FRAME_WIDTH/HEIGHT on the capture. Nothing stops an update from arriving during a recording.

Connect/startup handshake: CameraGroup.start calls the synchronous CameraManager.start, which runs time.sleep(0.25) before each worker.start() on Windows, inside the async call. Each worker opens cv2, publishes DeviceExtractedConfigMessage, then polls shm_subscription every 10 ms. The main process awaits every extracted config (100 ms polls), creates CameraGroupSharedMemory from them (its own handle is read_only=True and it is the 'original' that later unlinks), and publishes SetShmMessage once. Each camera recreates its ring with read_only=False, sets connected, and drains frames with cap.read() plus wait_10ms until all_ready.

Pause/unpause command: GET /skellycam/camera/group/all/pause_unpause toggles every camera's should_pause (unpause if any camera is paused, otherwise pause) and awaits the cameras' is_paused acknowledgement. CameraGroupManager.pause_all_groups and unpause_all_groups call camera_group.pause and camera_group.unpause, but CameraGroup only defines pause_unpause, so those calls would raise AttributeError. Nothing in skellycam or FreeMoCap calls them; only tests/conftest.py mocks them.

Close command: DELETE /skellycam/camera/group/close/all -> CameraGroup.close. It first stops any active recording, then sets shutdown_camera_group_flag. CameraManager.close then calls orchestrator.close, which sets should_close on every camera and spins in time.sleep(0.1) until every status.closed flag is set. That spin has no timeout and no process-liveness check. Only after it come join (3 s), terminate (3 s) and kill (2 s). All of this runs synchronously on the FastAPI asyncio thread. Finally the shm is unlinked.

Shutdown command: GET /shutdown sets global_kill_flag, awaits 100 ms and sends SIGTERM to its own process. The signal handler sets server.should_exit (main() installs one; uvicorn may install its own while serving, with the same effect), and main()'s finally calls WorkerRegistry.shutdown_all (kill flag -> join 3 s -> terminate -> join 3 s -> kill). The registry's child-monitor thread also SIGTERMs the parent when any worker dies with a non-zero exit code (unless it is marked _intentionally_terminated), or when anything sets global_kill_flag.

Failure escalation is app-wide. Any exception in the camera loop calls ipc.kill_everything() (global_kill_flag=True) and re-raises. Every camera worker exit also sets shutdown_camera_group_flag in its finally block. ManagedProcess's entry point sets global_kill_flag on an unhandled exception, on SIGTERM/SIGINT, and through an atexit safety net on unclean exit. All four websocket tasks set global_kill_flag on unexpected exceptions.

Grab-failure path: the retry loop exits after MAX_FAIL_COUNT=30 attempts within one frame (or when should_continue goes False) even if frame_success is still False, and the code never checks frame_success afterwards. It still calls put_frame and handle_video_recording with a frame whose frame_number was not incremented, because the increment only happens on success. It also sets frame_count to that same un-incremented number. For a recording camera, _validate_frame_number raises ValueError, which leads to kill_everything. For a non-recording camera, the ring write index moves ahead of the frame number (see missed facts).

check_framerate_reset is a self-triggered control action inside the frame loop. It hardcodes a 30 fps target, so the limit is 2 x 33.3 ms = 66.7 ms. The window it measures runs from just after opencv_get_frame returns (post-retrieve plus text overlay, previous_tik at L80-82) to after this camera's shm copy and record step. It therefore excludes lockstep waiting and other cameras. After frame 100, if that window exceeds the limit for more than 30 consecutive frames, the loop releases and re-creates the cv2.VideoCapture inline. There is no recording guard, the new config is not republished, and frame_rec_array is not reallocated.

claim_verdicts.final_statement: The websocket (/skellycam/websocket/connect) carries no commands. Client to server: only JSON containing frameNumber (with optional displayImageSizes), plus ping/pong. Server to client: binary frame payloads (the relay polls every 10 ms and sends only once the last sent frame is acknowledged, skipping one extra cycle after backpressure), framerate_update (at most about 4 Hz), app_state (sent when changed, checked every 1 s) and log records. skellycam-ui sends {type:'frameAcknowledgment', frameNumber} and never sends displayImageSizes (grep finds none in skellycam-ui/src). On every ack the server overwrites _display_image_sizes with data.get('displayImageSizes', None).

UI endpoint map: skellycam-ui defines health, shutdown, detect, group/apply, group/close/all, group/all/record/start, group/all/record/stop and group/all/pause_unpause. It also defines updateConfigs=/skellycam/camera/update, in useAppUrls.ts and again in server-helpers/server-urls.ts. camera_router (prefix /camera, mounted under /skellycam) has no such route: it defines detect, microphone/detect, group/apply, group/all/record/start, group/all/record/stop, group/close/all and group/all/pause_unpause. grep finds no caller of updateConfigs in skellycam-ui/src.

The metadata that travels with each frame lives in the same shm ring slot as the pixels: frame_metadata = camera_info (camera_id U128, camera_index, rotation, color_channels), frame_number, timebase_mapping and 9 lifecycle timestamps, 632 B in total (verified in verify_copies_output.txt). The ring write index doubles as the frame number. latest_frame_number returns last_written_index, latest_multiframe_number is the min across cameras, and readers index the ring by frame number. The invariant index == frame_number holds only if every put_frame follows a successful frame increment: both start at -1, and the first frame is 0.

Because of the order in which timestamps are written, shm readers (UI, FreeMoCap) never see the later lifecycle stamps. pre_copy_to_camera_shm_ns is set before put_frame, but post_copy_to_camera_shm_ns and pre/post_frame_record_ns are set after the frame is already in shm, and initialize_frame_recarray then resets them to 0 for the next frame. Only the recorder's per-frame metadata copy, taken after the write, contains all 9 timestamps.

How camera configs move. Requested config: HTTP body, passed into the worker kwargs at process start. Actual config: the EXTRACTED_CONFIG queue. Full configs for readers: inside CameraGroupSharedMemoryDTO through SetShmMessage. Slim per-frame camera_info: inside every ring slot. The writer fps used by VideoRecorder is 1/median of the last (up to 1000) loop intervals, computed once at least 30 exist, and passed in when the recorder is created (falling back to config.framerate if None). See missed facts for a bias in how those intervals are measured.

Stopping a recording pauses the group while it is still recording, so the tail of every recording contains a time gap that no frame-number check can see. Code-traced. stop_recording awaits pause (10 ms polls) before it sets last = max+3 and unpauses. Frames up to the pause and the 3 frames grabbed after the unpause are recorded with consecutive frame numbers. Likewise, the UI's /group/all/pause_unpause can be called during a recording; nothing guards it. The cameras stop grabbing while recording_in_progress stays True, and recording resumes with consecutive frame numbers after an arbitrarily long gap.

The measured framerate passed to VideoRecorder as the container fps is biased high. Code-traced inference, not measured. previous_tik is reset at the end of each iteration (L117), after put_frame, recording and check_framerate_reset. Each logged interval therefore runs from the end of the previous iteration to post-retrieve, and leaves out the previous frame's processing time. For a camera-bound loop the logged interval is about the sensor period minus the processing time, so the median fps is over-reported. No reference to fps or framerate appears in recording_finalizer.py (grep), so whether the finalizer corrects the container fps was not established.

Contention is modest. The control poll (about 20-40 us) is small next to the 16.7 ms frame budget at 60 fps; the 0.5 ms sleep granularity and the serialised lockstep matter more. The join/terminate/kill escalation in CameraManager.close only runs after that spin returns. risk_verdicts.risk: Encoding runs inside the capture loop, and frame_count is bumped only after the encode, so the lockstep orchestrator makes the group's frame period at least the slowest camera's grab+retrieve+putText+shm copy+encode. The shm copy alone measured 1.35 ms at 1080p and 0.60 ms at 720p (verify_copies_output.txt V2). On top of that comes a wake-up latency of up to about 0.5 ms (median real length of wait_10us; expected value around 0.26 ms, inferred). Capture and encode cannot overlap. At 5 x 60 fps the whole chain must fit in about 16.7 ms on the slowest camera.

Each frame-loop iteration does about 45 lock-protected Value reads with 5 cameras: 35 ready flags and 5 frame_counts in should_grab_by_id with no short-circuit, plus should_continue and the pause/close flags. It also does 2 Queue.empty() pipe peeks (8.9 us each) and beartype-wrapped calls. Cross-process contention is now measured (verify_lock_contention_output.txt): should_grab_by_id costs 17.3 us alone, 20.6 us with 5 processes spinning, and 33.7 us when interleaved with sleep(1e-5) as in the real loop. That is real but small against a 16.7 ms frame budget; the sleep granularity and lockstep matter more. RawValue reads cost 35 ns versus 306 ns.

If a single frame's 30 retries all fail, the retry loop exits without checking frame_success, and the stale, un-incremented frame is still written to shm and recorded. During a recording, _validate_frame_number raises, kill_everything runs and the whole app shuts down mid-recording; the current file is closed in the finally block, but the session ends. Without a recording, the ring index and frame number fall permanently out of step, which makes the websocket relay's get_latest_multiframe raise and set global_kill_flag (see missed facts).

check_framerate_reset hardcodes a 30 fps target. Its window covers only this camera's post-retrieve, shm copy and record time; lockstep waiting is excluded. So it fires only if this camera's own copy plus encode exceeds 66.7 ms for 31 consecutive frames after frame 100, for example with a very slow software encoder at 1080p. When it fires, it releases and reopens the camera inline with no recording guard, which stalls the whole group for the reopen, plus 1 s waits per failed attempt in create_cv2_video_capture, during an active recording. The reopened capture is not republished and frame_rec_array is not reallocated.

Config updates (/group/apply on an existing group) are not blocked during recording. They run inline in the frame loop with updating=True, which halts all cameras: 99 cap.read() calls in RECOMMEND exposure mode on non-Linux. A resolution change does NOT make the recorder's shape check raise. frame_rec_array keeps its old shape, cv2 retrieve writes the new-size frame into a newly allocated array that the code discards (V6), and stale pixels are silently written to shm and disk. Only a rotation change to 90 or 270 degrees would raise in _validate_image_shape and kill the app.

Every failure escalates to the whole app. Any camera-loop exception, any websocket task error (including the relay's frame-number-mismatch ValueError), or any non-zero worker exit sets global_kill_flag, and the server SIGTERMs itself. A UI or relay bug can therefore end a recording. Separately, there are no timeouts on finalize_recording, on the camera-side wait for all cameras to start recording, or on orchestrator.close's spin on closed flags. The last one can hang the event loop forever if a camera process dies without running its finally block.

Finishing a long recording stalls the camera loop. RecordingFinishedMessage.__post_init__ took 387 ms for 36,000 frames, plus writer.release(), plus 127 ms of pickling in the queue feeder thread (same GIL). frame_count is bumped only afterwards, so the group freezes. This happens after the last recorded frame, so it delays the live stream and FreeMoCap rather than disk writes. The main asyncio thread then unpickles about 24 MB per camera (98 ms each), which stalls the websocket relay and other HTTP handlers.

put_data copies every frame twice, copy(data) and then the slot assignment: 1.354 ms versus 0.15-0.17 ms for a single copy at 1080p, and 0.598 ms versus 0.07-0.08 ms at 720p (verify_copies_output.txt V2). The main-process UI relay copies all N full frames out of shm on every send, and because if_newer_than is ignored it also re-copies frames it has already sent.

Main-process control handlers block the asyncio event loop with synchronous sleeps and joins: CameraManager.start sleeps 0.25 s per camera, orchestrator.close spins on time.sleep(0.1) with no timeout, and the joins can take up to 3+3+2 s. This freezes websocket delivery and other HTTP calls during connect and close, and orchestrator.close can freeze it forever (see missed facts). Disk writes are not directly affected, because recording runs in the camera processes.

map.area: UI tap: SkellyCam UI (skellycam-ui Electron/React) and its server side (FastAPI websocket relay)
map.summary: The SkellyCam UI gets frames from one asyncio task, WebsocketServer._frontend_image_relay, which runs on the uvicorn event loop in the FastAPI process. Every 10 ms it checks one thing: has the client acknowledged the last frame it was sent? If so, it copies the latest complete multiframe (all cameras, full resolution) out of the shared-memory ring buffers into recarrays owned by the process. It then downscales each image to a fixed 0.5 scale (the client never sends displayImageSizes), JPEG-encodes it with OpenCV at quality 60 and packs everything into one binary message (24 B header, then a 56 B header plus JPEG per camera, then a 24 B footer). That message goes out over a websocket served by uvicorn's websockets-legacy protocol, which has permessage-deflate enabled by default. In the browser, the message arrives as an ArrayBuffer. The latest one is held in a single slot and picked up once per requestAnimationFrame tick. It is transferred without copying to a decode Web Worker (Blob, then createImageBitmap). The decoded ImageBitmaps are transferred to one OffscreenCanvas worker per camera, which draws them with bitmaprenderer.transferFromImageBitmap. Only after that dispatch does the client send a JSON ack {type:'frameAcknowledgment', frameNumber}. So the flow is stop-and-wait (the server waits for each ack), the latest frame always wins, and each server stage is synchronous on the event loop. At 5x1080p, building the payload measured 7-17.5 ms per multiframe and copying from shared memory 2.3-2.8 ms. The same connection carries logs (TRACE and above), app state (1 Hz, sent only when changed), framerate stats (about 4 Hz) and ping/pong. If any of those tasks hits an unexpected exception, including a malformed JSON message from the client, global_kill_flag is set and the whole app shuts down. The 777b058c commit FreeMoCap runs has the same source tree as 23ccbf20.

claims.statement: The UI websocket endpoint is /skellycam/websocket/connect. The router prefix /websocket plus route /connect is mounted under /{package_name}, and the client builds ws://host:port/skellycam/websocket/connect. Each connection creates one WebsocketServer and awaits run().

Each connection runs four asyncio tasks on one event loop: an image relay, a log relay, a client message handler and an app-state sender. Every send goes through one asyncio.Lock (_send_lock), so frame, log, state and framerate messages queue behind each other on the socket.

The UI tap reads shared memory inside the FastAPI/uvicorn server process. CameraGroup.start() creates CameraGroupSharedMemory there with read_only=True, and uvicorn serves the app from that same process, so the image relay runs on the main asyncio loop.

Frame selection works like this. The relay polls every 10 ms (await_10ms = asyncio.sleep(0.01), which measured 10.2-10.4 ms median on this Windows ProactorEventLoop). It only builds a payload once the client's last ack is >= last_sent_frame_number (stop-and-wait). After any poll that found the client un-acked, it deliberately skips one more poll.

The if_newer_than argument is passed down but never used. CameraGroup.get_latest_frontend_payload ignores it and always encodes the current latest multiframe. So if the client acks before the cameras produce a new frame, the server re-encodes and re-sends the same frame_number. This is a conclusion from reading the code; it was not observed on the wire.

The 'latest' frame is the minimum last_written_index across all cameras. get_latest_multiframe reads that index from every camera's ring buffer with get_data_by_index, which np.copyto's the whole slot (metadata plus full-resolution image) into a recarray cached per camera. If frame numbers disagree across cameras it raises ValueError.

The UI read path never touches last_read_index; get_data_by_index only reads last_written_index. So the UI tap cannot affect the writer's overwrite check, which compares against last_read_index. The only guard against reading a slot that has been lapped is the 'write_head - index >= ring_buffer_length' check. The ring holds 1 GiB per camera: about 172 slots at 1080p BGR and about 388 at 720p (1 GiB / itemsize).

I confirmed that the shared-memory read is a real copy. After get_data_by_index, np.shares_memory(cache.image, ring_shm.buffer) is False. Copying 5 cameras took 0.87-4.94 ms per multiframe at 720p and 2.33-2.76 ms at 1080p across two runs.
Images are rotated at full resolution before resizing. When camera_info.rotation != -1, cv2.rotate runs on the full-res image (an extra full-frame copy) and only then is the image downscaled.
Resize uses image_scale = 0.5 with cv2.INTER_LINEAR. If displayImageSizes is supplied, the scale becomes min(display_w/w, display_h/h, 0.5), which keeps the aspect ratio and never goes above 0.5.

The skellycam-ui client never sends displayImageSizes. Its only ack is {type:'frameAcknowledgment', frameNumber}. The server reads data.get('displayImageSizes', None), which becomes None after every ack, so every camera is always sent at 0.5 scale (960x540 for 1080p, 640x360 for 720p) whatever size the canvas is.

Encoding is OpenCV cv2.imencode('.jpg') at a fixed IMWRITE_JPEG_QUALITY of 60. The result is turned into Python bytes with jpeg_data.tobytes() and then copied into a module-global reusable bytearray, sized (n_cams+1) MiB + 300*n_cams and grown if needed.

Wire format: one binary websocket message per camera group per send. It is a payload header (u1 message_type=0, i8 frame_number, i4 number_of_cameras; 24 B with align=True), then for each camera a 56 B frame header (type=1, frame_number, S16 camera_id, camera_index, width, height, color_channels, jpeg_string_length) followed by the JPEG bytes, then a 24 B footer (type=2). A dtype check script confirmed the 24/56 B sizes and offsets, and they match the TS constants.

The returned payload is a copy. create_frontend_payload returns _reusable_bytes_payload[:current_pos], and slicing a bytearray allocates a new bytearray, so the whole payload is copied once more. A test confirmed bytearray[:n] is a copy, costing 1.0-5.7 us per slice for 44-80 KiB payloads.

Payload build cost for 5 cameras, synthetic gradient-plus-noise BGR (so JPEGs are only about 9-16 KiB per camera, smaller than real scenes): 3.5-8.9 ms per multiframe at 1280x720, and 7-17.5 ms at 1920x1080 across runs and the profiler. At 1080p each camera costs about 0.6-1.8 ms resize and 1.2-1.5 ms imencode. cProfile shows imencode and resize dominate, with about 20 ms of Python and recarray attribute overhead per 30 calls.

The encode is synchronous on the event loop. _frontend_image_relay is a coroutine that calls the plain function get_latest_frontend_payloads, then create_frontend_payload, with no executor or thread offload. The shared-memory copy, resize and JPEG encode therefore block the uvicorn loop, which also serves HTTP control endpoints and the websocket receive handler.

Transport: starlette send_bytes passes the bytearray to uvicorn's ASGI send. uvicorn 0.44 'auto' picks the websockets-legacy WebSocketServerProtocol whenever websockets (16.0) is installed. Legacy send() calls write_frame, then Frame.serialize, which writes the header and data into an io.BytesIO and returns getvalue(), and then transport.write. That is at least one more user-space copy of the payload before the kernel copy.

uvicorn has ws_per_message_deflate=True by default, and SkellyCam's uvicorn.Config does not override it, so the server offers permessage-deflate (zlib at its default level). If a client negotiates it, every JPEG payload is zlib-compressed on the event loop. Measured cost: 1.7 ms (5x720p) and 5.6-6.7 ms (5x1080p) per payload, for about a 47% size cut on synthetic images. Real JPEG data would compress far less.

Backpressure is purely application level. When a client is slow, the server simply stops producing payloads (no queue builds up) and logs a TRACE warning when the un-acked gap passes 1000 frames. There is no drop counter beyond that. The transport's drain() also awaits the socket buffer.

Side channels on the same socket. Framerate: a FramerateUpdateMessage (server capture fps from frame_number and timestamp deltas, plus 'Display' send rate) goes out about every 0.25 s and resets the trackers. Logs: every record at TRACE and above is sent as msgspec JSON. App state: the CGM state dict is sent every 1 s when it changes. Ping/pong: the client sends 'ping' every 30 s and the server replies 'pong'.

Two declared outputs are never sent. WebsocketMessageType.PERFORMANCE_DATA exists, and CameraGroupManager.get_latest_performance_data (which would do another full get_latest_frames copy) has no caller in the websocket server or anywhere else in skellycam. CameraGroup.get_frontend_payload_by_frame_number also has no caller.
The client opens the socket with binaryType='arraybuffer', so each binary message arrives as an ArrayBuffer. JSON acks are sent with JSON.stringify.

Client frame selection: onmessage stores the newest ArrayBuffer in pendingPayloadRef, overwriting any older one. A requestAnimationFrame loop starts at most one decode at a time, at most once per rAF tick, and skips decoding while the stream is paused. UI decode starts are therefore capped at the display refresh rate.
FrameProcessor hands the ArrayBuffer to an inline Blob-URL Web Worker through postMessage with a transfer list, which detaches it on the main thread without copying.

The decode worker parses headers with a DataView. It then decodes the JPEGs one after another: a Uint8Array view, then new Blob([view]) (which copies the JPEG bytes into the Blob), then createImageBitmap(blob, {premultiplyAlpha:'none', colorSpaceConversion:'none'}). The resulting ImageBitmaps are posted back to the main thread as transferables. The protocol constants are duplicated by hand inside the worker string.
binary-frame-parser.ts parseMultiFramePayload, a main-thread parser that decodes in parallel, is only re-exported from services/server/index.ts and never called. The live path is the worker.

Rendering: each CameraView canvas is handed to its own worker through transferControlToOffscreen. Frames reach that worker as transferred ImageBitmaps. The worker keeps only the newest pending bitmap (closing any it drops), resizes the canvas to the bitmap's size, and draws inside its own requestAnimationFrame loop using a 'bitmaprenderer' context and transferFromImageBitmap, with no pixel copy. CSS object-fit 'contain' then scales the canvas.

The ack (the server's only flow control) is sent once the decoded bitmaps have been posted to the renderer workers, not once they are painted, and it carries the maximum frameNumber in the payload. The display fps the client shows is computed per camera from the gap between decode results on the main thread, so a re-sent duplicate frame would count toward it.

Opening the Playback tab calls setStreamPaused(true). The rAF loop then stops decoding and acking, so after one more payload the server stops encoding because of the ack gate. Playback video comes from FileResponse over HTTP, not from the ring buffer.

Where SkellyCam feeds FreeMoCap's UI: when no realtime pipeline is active, FreeMoCap's application calls SkellyCam's CameraGroupManager.get_latest_frontend_payloads directly. FreeMoCap's camera-only UI therefore gets the same 0.5-scale, q60 JPEG payload, built on FreeMoCap's own event loop.

An unexpected exception in any websocket task sets the global kill flag, which shuts the app down. That covers the image relay, log relay, state sender and client handler. A client text message that starts with '{' but is not valid JSON raises ValueError, which reaches that path. So does the cross-camera frame-number mismatch ValueError in get_latest_multiframe.

[sibling-prior-art, skellycam-shm-ui fork, not the code under study] Commit 754962df adds a second named shared-memory ring of raw BGR for the Electron main process. The writer is called inside the websocket relay loop after the normal JPEG payload is built. UIShmWriter re-reads the frames with get_images_by_frame_number (another full copy), calls raw_image.tobytes() (another full copy), then write_frame copies into the UI shared memory (a third copy per camera). The JPEG payload is still encoded even when shared memory is the only consumer.

[sibling-prior-art] Electron main maps the shared memory with koffi MapViewOfFile, polls it every 16 ms, and forwards each frame to the renderer with webContents.postMessage('shm-frame', {data: frame.data.buffer}, [frame.data.buffer]). frame.data is a Buffer view onto the mapped region. Sending from the main process to the renderer process crosses a process boundary, so the pixels are copied again. Whether .buffer sends just the slot or the entire mapping is unverified.

[sibling-prior-art] The fork's renderer converts raw BGR to RGBA with a per-pixel JavaScript loop on the main thread, then calls createImageBitmap(ImageData). The loop assigns rgba[dstOff] twice and never assigns rgba[dstOff+2], so colours would come out wrong.

[sibling-prior-art] Commit e95a198f adds a control shared-memory ring (32 slots x 8 KB) for logs, framerate and app state. When an SHM reader is present, the websocket server skips sending frames and control messages over the websocket and writes them to shared memory instead.

frame_copies.where: Server: SHM ring slot -> process-local cached recarray (get_latest_multiframe -> get_data_by_index), every camera, full resolution
frame_copies.necessary: Partly. The copy gives a stable snapshot, so the writer can't overwrite the slot mid-encode. It is also the largest copy on the UI path: 31 MB per multiframe at 5x1080p, measured 2.3-2.8 ms. cv2.resize can read straight from a view of the SHM slot and check the frame number afterwards, because the ring holds about 172 slots at 1080p. That would remove the copy.

frame_copies.where: Server: cv2.rotate of the full-res image when rotation is configured
frame_copies.necessary: Avoidable. Rotating after the resize would work on a quarter of the pixels. Rotating on the client, with a CSS transform or by drawing the bitmap rotated, would remove it entirely.

frame_copies.where: Server: cv2.resize to 0.5 scale (reads full res, writes a new half-res array)
frame_copies.necessary: Needed to shrink the payload. It could reuse a preallocated dst buffer, and the scale could follow the real canvas size if the client sent displayImageSizes.

frame_copies.where: Server: cv2.imencode('.jpg', q=60)
frame_copies.necessary: Needed for a remote browser client. A local Electron client could take raw or GPU-shared frames instead (see the sibling prior art). Encoding costs 1.2-1.5 ms per 960x540 camera on synthetic images.

frame_copies.where: Server: jpeg_data.tobytes()
frame_copies.necessary: Avoidable. Assigning the numpy buffer, or a memoryview of it, straight into the bytearray slice would skip this copy.

frame_copies.where: Server: copy JPEG and headers into the module-global _reusable_bytes_payload
frame_copies.necessary: Needed to assemble one message (or use scatter/gather writes). Combined with the tobytes copy, every JPEG is copied twice.

frame_copies.where: Server: return _reusable_bytes_payload[:current_pos]
frame_copies.kind: memcpy (whole payload; bytearray slice confirmed to copy)
frame_copies.necessary: Avoidable with memoryview(buf)[:n]. That is safe here because the send is awaited before the next build.

frame_copies.where: Server: permessage-deflate zlib compress (only if the client negotiates it; uvicorn offers it by default)
frame_copies.necessary: Unnecessary for JPEG payloads. Turning it off (uvicorn ws_per_message_deflate=False) saves 1.7-6.7 ms per payload on the event loop.

frame_copies.where: Server: websockets legacy Frame.serialize writes the header and payload into io.BytesIO, then getvalue(), then transport.write (kernel socket buffer)
frame_copies.necessary: Comes with the library. At least one user-space copy plus the kernel copy. A websocket stack that does vectored writes would avoid the user-space copy.

frame_copies.where: Client: the browser receives the websocket message into an ArrayBuffer (binaryType='arraybuffer')
frame_copies.necessary: Needed over a websocket.

frame_copies.where: Client: main thread -> decode worker postMessage with a transfer list
frame_copies.necessary: Already zero-copy.

frame_copies.where: Client decode worker: new Blob([Uint8Array view]) per camera
frame_copies.necessary: Avoidable. WebCodecs ImageDecoder, or createImageBitmap on a Blob built once per payload, would decode from the bytes without this copy.

frame_copies.where: Client decode worker: createImageBitmap(blob) JPEG decode
frame_copies.necessary: Needed as long as the wire format is JPEG.

frame_copies.where: Client: ImageBitmap transfers (decode worker -> main -> per-camera renderer worker) and transferFromImageBitmap into the canvas
frame_copies.necessary: Already zero-copy.

flow_steps.action: write frames into the per-camera SHM ring and bump last_written_index (other area)
flow_steps.to: FastAPI server process / uvicorn asyncio loop

flow_steps.process_or_thread: FastAPI server process / asyncio task WebsocketFrontendImageRelay

risks_for_priorities.risk: An unexpected exception in a UI websocket task sets global_kill_flag, which shuts the app down and with it any recording in progress. That includes a malformed '{...' text message from any client (ValueError from json.loads) and a frame-number mismatch ValueError in get_latest_multiframe. A display problem can therefore end a disk recording.

For the record, this one is safe: the UI reader does not advance last_read_index, so a slow or absent UI cannot make the writer's overwrite check fail or block it. The UI tap is decoupled from the sequential consumers that feed the disk.

The shared-memory copy, resize, JPEG encode and (if negotiated) zlib deflate all run synchronously on the single uvicorn event loop. That is about 10-26 ms per multiframe at 5x1080p from the measured components (2.3-2.8 copy + 7-17.5 build + up to 6.7 deflate). While it runs, HTTP control endpoints and websocket receive are blocked, and the UI can never keep up with 5x60 fps.

Display throughput is cut by several latencies in series. Stop-and-wait means one payload in flight per ack. Polling is every 10 ms, plus one extra skipped poll after any un-acked check. Decode starts only on rAF ticks, and the ack waits for decode. The UI rate is therefore set by the round-trip time and the display refresh, not by the camera fps. End-to-end UI fps was not measured.
if_newer_than is ignored, so after a fast ack the server can re-encode and re-send a frame the client already has. That wastes encode time and inflates the display fps counters.
Logs at TRACE and above, framerate, state and frames all share one send lock and socket. Heavy logging competes with frames for the event loop and the socket.

Every UI payload copies all raw full-res frames out of shared memory (about 31 MB per multiframe at 5x1080p, about 1.9 GB/s at a 60 Hz UI) just to make 960x540 thumbnails. JPEG bytes are then copied three to four more times on the server (tobytes, assemble, slice, websocket serialize) and once in the browser (Blob).
The client never sends displayImageSizes, so small tiles still receive full 0.5-scale images. That means more resize and encode work and more bytes than needed.

verification.area: UI tap: SkellyCam UI (skellycam-ui Electron/React) and its server side (FastAPI websocket relay). Verified against skellycam 23ccbf20, freemocap 5632778a, and the venvs.

claim_verdicts.final_statement: The UI websocket endpoint is /skellycam/websocket/connect. APIRouter(prefix='/websocket') plus @websocket('/connect') is mounted with prefix /{skellycam.__package_name__}. The client builds ws://host:port + WS_PATH, with WS_PATH='/skellycam/websocket/connect' and default port 53117. Each connection accepts, creates one WebsocketServer and awaits run().

Each connection runs four asyncio tasks on one event loop: an image relay, a log relay, a client message handler and an app-state sender. Every outbound send (_send_json, _send_bytes, _send_text, _send_msgspec_json) takes the same asyncio.Lock (_send_lock), so frame, log, state, framerate and pong messages are serialised on the socket.

The UI tap reads shared memory inside the uvicorn/FastAPI process. CameraGroup.start() (an async method on that process's loop) creates the original CameraGroupSharedMemory there with read_only=True and publishes its DTO to the camera processes. uvicorn.Server(config).serve() runs in the same process with no workers, so the image relay is a coroutine on the main asyncio loop.

Frame selection: the relay awaits asyncio.sleep(0.01) each loop (median 10.23-10.34 ms on this Windows ProactorEventLoop over two runs). It builds a payload only when last_received_frontend_confirmation >= last_sent_frame_number (stop-and-wait; always true before the first send). After any poll that found the client un-acked it sets skipped_previous, so the next acked poll is skipped too. In practice the server waits at least about 20 ms after an ack that arrives late.

if_newer_than is accepted by CameraGroupManager.get_latest_frontend_payloads and passed to CameraGroup.get_latest_frontend_payload, which never uses it and always encodes the current latest multiframe. If the client acks before a new multiframe exists, the server re-encodes and re-sends the same frame_number. This is inferred from the code and was not observed on the wire.

The 'latest' multiframe is min(last_written_index) across cameras (latest_frame_number returns last_written_index.value). get_latest_multiframe calls get_data_by_index(target) on every camera's ring, and that np.copyto's the whole slot (metadata plus full-resolution image) into a recarray cached per camera in self._latest_frames. If the frame_numbers read back disagree it raises ValueError.

The UI read path (get_data_by_index) only reads last_written_index and never touches last_read_index. That decoupling exists, but it does not protect the disk path. In production nothing advances last_read_index: get_next_data/retrieve_next_frame are called only from tests, diagnostics and the module's __main__. The only writer, opencv_camera_loop, calls put_frame(overwrite=True), so _check_for_overwrite is never enforced. The ring is a free-running overwrite ring. The only lapping guard on the read side is 'write_head - index >= ring_buffer_length', checked BEFORE the np.copyto with no re-check afterwards (time-of-check/time-of-use). The 1 GiB per camera ring holds 172 slots at 1080p BGR (itemsize 6,221,432 B, about 2.87 s at 60 fps) and 388 slots at 720p (itemsize 2,765,432 B, about 6.47 s at 60 fps).
claim_verdicts.note: Slot counts were reproduced by uitap_verify_copies.py (V1). The overwrite flag and the missing last_read_index consumers were found by grep over skellycam/ (callers: opencv_camera_loop.py:96 only, overwrite=True).

claim_verdicts.final_statement: The shared-memory read is a real copy: after get_data_by_index, np.shares_memory(cache.image, ring_shm.buffer) is False. Copying 5 cameras measured 0.87 and 4.94 ms per multiframe at 720p and 2.33 and 2.76 ms at 1080p over two runs. Caveats: the benchmark re-reads the same slot of a 4-slot ring, so the source is cache-warm. The 4.94 ms at 720p was the first measurement in run 1 and probably includes first-touch effects. Neither number reflects a cold read from a large ring.

When camera_info.rotation != -1, cv2.rotate runs on the full-resolution image (a new full-size array) before the 0.5 downscale. Measured per camera at 1080p: rotate-then-resize 2.07 ms vs resize-then-rotate 0.67 ms.

Resize uses image_scale = 0.5 with cv2.INTER_LINEAR. If displayImageSizes has an entry for the camera, scale = min(display_w/orig_w, display_h/orig_h, 0.5), which keeps the aspect ratio and never exceeds 0.5.

skellycam-ui never sends displayImageSizes: grep over skellycam-ui/src finds no occurrence. Its only ack is {type:'frameAcknowledgment', frameNumber}. On every ack the server sets _display_image_sizes = data.get('displayImageSizes', None), which is None, so every camera is sent at 0.5 scale (960x540 for 1080p, 640x360 for 720p) whatever the canvas size.

Encoding is cv2.imencode('.jpg') with IMWRITE_JPEG_QUALITY fixed at 60. The ndarray result is turned into bytes with jpeg_data.tobytes() and then slice-assigned into the module-global _reusable_bytes_payload. That buffer is sized (n_cams+1)*1 MiB + 300*n_cams and grown with extend() if needed. It is one buffer per process, shared by every connection and camera group.

Wire format: one binary websocket message per camera group per send. It is a 24 B payload header (u1 message_type=0, i8 frame_number at offset 8, i4 number_of_cameras at offset 16; align=True), then per camera a 56 B frame header (type=1, frame_number, S16 camera_id at 16, camera_index at 32, width at 36, height at 40, color_channels at 44, jpeg_string_length at 48) followed by the JPEG bytes, then a 24 B footer (type=2). The dtype check confirms the sizes and offsets, and they match binary-protocol.ts and the constants duplicated in the decode worker. Note: the header recarrays are created with np.recarray(1, ...) without zeroing, so padding bytes are uninitialised (harmless).

create_frontend_payload returns _reusable_bytes_payload[:current_pos]. Slicing a bytearray allocates a new bytearray, so the whole payload is copied once more. Measured 1.0-5.7 us per slice for 44-80 KiB payloads (negligible in time).

Payload build cost for 5 cameras with synthetic gradient-plus-noise BGR: 3.53 and 8.92 ms per multiframe at 1280x720, and 12.76 and 17.51 ms at 1920x1080 in two runs; the cProfile run shows 7.1 ms (0.212 s / 30). Per camera at 1080p: resize 0.57-1.79 ms and imencode 0.67-1.52 ms (bench and profiler). The function's own Python time is about 20 ms per 30 calls (about 0.7 ms per call), plus recarray __getattribute__/__setattr__. beartype_this_package() is active in skellycam, so the beartype wrapper is included in these timings, as it would be in production. Synthetic images are easy to compress (about 9-16 KiB per camera after the resize). A higher-entropy blurred-noise 960x540 image produced an 84.8 KiB JPEG (2.8x larger) and took 0.86 ms vs 0.65 ms to encode, so real scenes probably cost more bytes and modestly more encode time.

claim_verdicts.final_statement: The build is synchronous on the event loop. _frontend_image_relay is a coroutine that directly calls the plain function CGM.get_latest_frontend_payloads, then CameraGroup.get_latest_frontend_payload, get_latest_frames (SHM copy) and create_frontend_payload (resize, encode, pack), with no run_in_executor or thread offload. The loop is blocked for the whole build, which delays async HTTP endpoints, the websocket receive handler and the other websocket tasks.

Transport in SkellyCam's venv (uvicorn 0.44.0, websockets 16.0, starlette 1.0.0): starlette send_bytes passes the bytearray to uvicorn's ASGI send. uvicorn 'auto' selects websockets_impl.WebSocketProtocol, which is built on websockets.legacy. Legacy send() calls prepare_data, which passes bytes-like data through unchanged, then write_frame, write_frame_sync and Frame.serialize. serialize writes the header and the payload into an io.BytesIO; that write is one user-space copy. getvalue() does not copy again on CPython 3.12.13: it returns the same object on repeated calls. The Proactor transport.write then passes the bytes through without a copy when idle (bytes(bytes) is identity), but copies into a bytearray buffer if an earlier write is still pending. So there is exactly one user-space copy in websockets, plus a conditional transport copy, plus the kernel copy. FreeMoCap's venv differs: uvicorn 0.51.0 'auto' selects websockets_sansio_impl.WebSocketsSansIOProtocol (websockets 16.1.1), so this analysis does not carry over when the server runs from that venv.

uvicorn.Config defaults ws_per_message_deflate=True, and SkellyCam's uvicorn.Config (host, port, log_level, reload only) does not override it. The protocol therefore registers ServerPerMessageDeflateFactory() with default compress_settings (zlib default level). If the client negotiates it, every payload is zlib-compressed synchronously on the event loop. Measured with zlib wbits=-15: 1.72-1.74 ms (5x720p) and 5.62-6.69 ms (5x1080p) per payload. Sizes fell 41-49% on the synthetic payloads (45421 to 23255 B; 82130 to 48603 B). That reduction is a quirk of the gradient images (34-38% even on one JPEG): a high-entropy blurred-noise JPEG shrank only 0.2-0.4%. On real camera JPEGs, deflate probably costs CPU for almost no saving.

Backpressure is application-level stop-and-wait with no timeout. While un-acked, the server produces nothing, so no queue builds. The TRACE warning (backpressure > 1000 and divisible by 1000) can essentially never fire: last_sent_frame_number only advances when a payload is sent, which requires an ack, so the gap stays bounded by how far frame numbers move between consecutive sends. There is no drop counter and no ack timeout. One lost ack, or a client that fails to ack, stalls the stream until reconnect. The transport's drain() also awaits socket-buffer flow control.

Side channels on the same socket. Framerate: inside the image-relay loop, every 0.25 s or more, it sends a FramerateUpdateMessage (server capture fps from frame_number and timestamp deltas, plus the 'Display' send rate), but only when both trackers have data, and then resets both. Logs: every queued record at TRACE and above is sent as msgspec JSON. App state: the CGM state dict is sent when it changes, checked every 1 s. Ping/pong: the client sends a text 'ping' every 30 s (heartbeatInterval 30000) and the server replies 'pong'. uvicorn also runs protocol-level pings (ws_ping_interval=20 s).

WebsocketMessageType.PERFORMANCE_DATA exists, and performance_data.py builds a message with it, but CameraGroupManager.get_latest_performance_data has no caller in skellycam/ outside its definition (that path would do another full get_latest_frames copy). extract_performance_data_from_frames is used only there and in tests. CameraGroup.get_frontend_payload_by_frame_number also has no caller.
The client sets ws.binaryType='arraybuffer', so binary messages arrive as ArrayBuffers. Non-string sends, such as the ack object, are JSON.stringify'd.

onmessage stores the newest ArrayBuffer in pendingPayloadRef, overwriting any older one. The rAF loop starts a decode only when not paused, not already processing, and a payload is pending. Because the next requestAnimationFrame is scheduled only after the awaited decode and dispatch finish, decodes are strictly serial and at most one starts per rAF tick. UI decode rate is therefore capped by the display refresh and by decode latency.
FrameProcessor creates an inline Blob-URL Web Worker and posts the ArrayBuffer with a transfer list ([data]), which detaches it on the main thread without copying.

The decode worker parses headers with a DataView. It then decodes the JPEGs sequentially: a Uint8Array view, new Blob([view]), then createImageBitmap(blob, {premultiplyAlpha:'none', colorSpaceConversion:'none', resizeQuality:'pixelated'}). The resulting ImageBitmaps are posted back as transferables. The protocol constants are duplicated by hand inside the worker string. That the Blob constructor copies the bytes comes from the Blob spec; the code does not show it and it was not measured here.

binary-frame-parser.ts parseMultiFramePayload (lines 54-251; it decodes in parallel and returns Promise.all) is only re-exported from services/server/index.ts and never called. The live path is the decode worker.

Each CameraView canvas is handed to its own worker through transferControlToOffscreen. Frames arrive as transferred ImageBitmaps. On arrival the worker resizes the canvas to the bitmap size if needed and keeps only the newest pending bitmap (closing any it replaces and counting framesDropped). Its own rAF loop draws with a 'bitmaprenderer' context via transferFromImageBitmap. CSS object-fit 'contain' scales the canvas.

The ack, the server's only flow control, is sent from dispatchFrames once the decoded bitmaps have been posted to the renderer workers, not once they are painted. It carries Math.max of the payload's frameNumbers. If processFramePayload rejects (decode-worker error) or resolves null, no ack is sent. The display fps the client shows is computed per camera on the main thread from the gap between decode results, so a re-sent duplicate frame would count toward it.

Opening the Playback route calls setStreamPaused(true), which sets isStreamPausedRef. The rAF loop then stops decoding and acking. After at most the one un-acked payload already in flight, the server stops building payloads because of the ack gate. Playback video is served by stream_video as a FileResponse over HTTP, not from the ring buffer. stream_video is a sync def that may first transcode a non-web-compatible file to H.264 (pyav/libx264) inside the server process.

When no realtime pipeline is alive, FreeMoCap's application calls SkellyCam's CameraGroupManager.get_latest_frontend_payloads directly and wraps each result in a FrontendImagePacket. FreeMoCap's camera-only UI therefore gets the same 0.5-scale, q60 JPEG payload (SHM copy, resize and encode included), built synchronously on FreeMoCap's own event loop. FreeMoCap's relay catches IndexError from this call and resets; SkellyCam's relay does not.

An unexpected exception in any of the four websocket tasks sets global_kill_flag. That flag makes CameraGroupIPC.should_continue False in every camera process, so camera loops exit and finish_recording runs in their finally blocks: an in-progress recording is cut short, not corrupted. Paths that reach it: (a) a client text message starting with '{' or '[' that is not valid JSON (json.JSONDecodeError re-raised as ValueError, caught by the generic handler); (b) a syntactically valid ack with a non-numeric frameNumber, e.g. "5", which is stored as-is and makes the int >= str comparison in check_frame_acknowledgment_status raise TypeError inside the relay's try (inferred from the code, not executed); (c) the cross-camera frame-number ValueError, or an IndexError from get_data_by_index, in get_latest_multiframe. Path (c) is unlikely in practice: target = min(last_written_index), and the orchestrator keeps cameras in lockstep, so a slot would have to be lapped by 172 or more frames.

[sibling-prior-art, skellycam-shm-ui fork, not the code under study] Commits 754962df and e95a198f add a second named shared-memory ring of raw BGR for the Electron main process. UIShmWriter.write_frames_from_camera_group is called inside the websocket relay after get_latest_frontend_payloads has already built the JPEG payload. It re-reads the frames with get_images_by_frame_number (another full np.copyto per camera), calls raw_image.tobytes() (another full copy), and write_frame slice-assigns into the UI SHM (a third full copy per camera). The JPEG payload is still encoded when shared memory is the only consumer; only the websocket send is skipped.

[sibling-prior-art] Electron main maps the shared memory with koffi MapViewOfFile(handle, FILE_MAP_ALL_ACCESS, 0, 0, 0), polls it every 16 ms, and posts each frame with webContents.postMessage('shm-frame', {..., data: frame.data.buffer}, [frame.data.buffer]). frame.data is Buffer.from(mappedView.buffer, offset, dataSize), a view, so frame.data.buffer is the ArrayBuffer underlying mappedView and not a slot-sized buffer. Whether that is the whole mapping, and whether an externally-backed ArrayBuffer can be transferred at all, is unverified. Crossing from the main process to the renderer process implies at least one copy.

[sibling-prior-art] The fork's renderer converts raw BGR to RGBA with a per-pixel JavaScript loop, then calls createImageBitmap(ImageData). The loop assigns rgba[dstOff] twice (first raw[srcOff+2], then raw[srcOff]) and never assigns rgba[dstOff+2], so the red channel gets blue and blue is 0.

When the control writer has a reader, the websocket server skips sending frames, framerate, logs and app state over the websocket and writes them to shared memory instead.
